Scientists Uncover a Potential Root Cause of the Global Allergy Epidemic

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have identified a potential biological mechanism that could explain how seemingly unrelated environmental factors contribute to the growing prevalence of allergies.
  • Allergies may begin with an energy crisis inside the cells that protect the body from the outside world, rather than a malfunction of the immune system.
  • Industry observers note that the researchers identified abnormalities involving mitochondria, the structures responsible for producing much of the energy cells need to function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have identified a potential biological mechanism that could explain how seemingly unrelated environmental factors contribute to the growing prevalence of allergies.

Allergies may begin with an energy crisis inside the cells that protect the body from the outside world, rather than a malfunction of the immune system. An extensive analysis led by Griffith University researchers challenges decades of conventional thinking about allergic diseases and proposes a potential biological origin for conditions ranging from eczema to food allergies.

Industry observers note that the researchers identified abnormalities involving mitochondria, the structures responsible for producing much of the energy cells need to function. Their findings suggest that epithelial cells, which form protective barriers along the skin, gut, nose, lungs, and esophagus, may struggle to meet environmental and metabolic demands, triggering an excessive immune response.

“For 60 years, we’ve taught that allergies start with the immune system and the barrier breaks as a consequence, but our work suggests it may be the other way around,” said study lead Professor Peter Smith, a clinical immunologist from Griffith’s School of Medicine and Dentistry.

The team examined what it describes as the largest collection of multi-omic allergy data known to the researchers, drawing on 116 case-control cohorts and data from 3,776 patients. Multi-omic analysis combines different types of molecular information to identify biological patterns that might otherwise go undetected.

In a recent development, scientists may have discovered the hidden cause of allergies. Credit: Professor Peter Smith, Griffith University.

“Allergy diseases, which now affect up to one in three children, may start one step earlier as a power failure in the mitochondria of the epithelial cells which form the body’s barrier surfaces,” Professor Smith remarked.

“The barrier cell can’t meet the energy and stress demands of the modern environment so raises the alarm too easily, and the immune events we recognize as an allergy, follow.

“It could help to explain why some children have eczema, food allergies, hay fever, asthma and related conditions.”.

In a recent development, the strongest evidence emerged in eosinophilic esophagitis, an allergic inflammatory disease affecting the esophagus. Across all 13 independent patient cohorts, researchers found reduced activity in the cellular process responsible for removing damaged mitochondria.

In patients with eczema, abnormalities affecting the skin’s protective barrier and antioxidant defenses appeared even in areas without inflammation. This finding is consistent with the possibility that cellular dysfunction precedes visible symptoms.

However, the mitochondrial signature was not universal. Researchers found only partial evidence of it in hay fever, while the pattern was absent in established asthma and nasal polyps.

The researchers propose that several environmental factors associated with allergies could converge on the same biological vulnerability: the ability of epithelial cells to generate sufficient energy and withstand stress.

Potential contributors include highly processed diets, air pollution, microplastics, detergents, declining dietary fiber intake, and antibiotic exposure early in life.

Associate Professor Nic West, a molecular immunologist from Griffith’s School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences and co-author of the study, noted the wide range of factors associated with allergies has made it difficult to develop a unified explanation for their rapid increase within a single generation.

The proposed mechanism could also explain why allergic diseases frequently recur after treatment. Inflammation itself can damage epithelial cells, potentially creating a self-perpetuating cycle of barrier dysfunction and immune activation.

“The research also explains why allergies can relapse,” Associate Professor West stated.

“Once inflammation is established it damages the barrier further.

“Today’s drugs act downstream, so the disease often returns when treatment stops as they do not reach the root cause.”.

According to recent reports, the researchers emphasize that their findings support a hypothesis rather than establish a definitive cause of allergies. Direct measurements of epithelial cell function before symptoms appear will be needed to determine whether mitochondrial dysfunction initiates allergic disease.

“We have spent our careers managing the smoke and for the first time we think we can see the fire, and it is not where everyone was looking,” Professor Smith said.

“This is not a cure but is something we have never had before – a logical starting point.

“The next step is to measure these cells directly in infants before the allergy develops.”.

Reference: “The Origins of Allergy: An Outside-In, Bioenergetic Hypothesis” by Peter K. Smith, Nicholas P. West, Stanley Du Preez, Hugh A. Sampson, Peter W. Hellings, David Price, Liam O’Mahony, Carina Venter, Cezmi A. Akdis and Gil Yosipovitch, 29 October 2026, Allergy. DOI: 10.1111/all.70532.

The Dutch manufacturer behind the appliance, Technivorm, really exercises what it calls its core tenets of “form and function,” and will service any repairs on the machines for up to five years. That is exactly the kind of lore I crave from the splurge-level items on my holiday shopping list (and the kind that will make your own design-savvy, coffee-loving giftee feel special).

Industry observers note that if you’re reaching into your budget for gifts that last, impress, and — if you’re giving them to a family member or partner — you might be able to use yourself for years to come, the fancy gifts for food lovers start getting good. There are the substantial-ticket kitchen titans: a high-tech Mill food recycler, sleek Miele vacuums (post-kitchen-prep cleanup doesn’t stand a chance), and electric pizza ovens that can reach 850 degrees Fahrenheit in just 90 seconds. Sometimes “splurges” are just wise investments, especially with appliances and cookware; your giftee is going to use a well-made cutting board or top-tier kitchen knife for years or decades to come. There are also the gifts with spectacular whimsy: a stationary exercise bike that makes smoothies, a martini-lover’s menorah, a tabletop lighter that’s also an incredible conversation piece.

In a recent development, these gifts may be at higher price points than a classic stocking stuffer, but they’re also extra-special — we’d say, so worth it if you have the dough. If you’re looking to roll out the red carpet with splurge-worthy food and kitchen gifts, look no further.

It has been revealed that the casual gift for someone who loves food and loves to host might be nice set of chip and dip bowls, cocktail napkins, or perhaps some beeswax candlesticks. No better way to pull focus at the dining table than with this copper and brass pepper mill, which East Fork notes can literally last for “hundreds of years” when cared for properly. This Balmuda Pro has an even more powerful heat source, and a setting called Salamander Grill Mode for giving your salmon the restaurant-grade finishing treatment.

  • The discovery is in research published in Astronomy and Astrophysics titled "Euclid: Discovery of a quasar at z = 8.13 hosting a 360-million-solar-mass black hole." The lead author is Julien Wolf, who was a postdoc at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy when the research was done.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quasars are the cosmos' most luminous objects, generated by supermassive black holes (SMBH) that are accreting enormous amounts of matter. Astronomers keep finding these massive objects further and further back in time. The ESA's Euclid just found the newest record holder: the telescope observed it 40 million years sooner than the previous record-holder, and it was found at redshift z=8.13, corresponding to about 630 million years after the Big Bang. That's firmly in the Epoch of Reionization.

The quasar's technical name is J1504+6252, but it's been given the more recognizable name DÃºn Aonghasa. DÃºn Aonghasa is an ancient stone fort on top of a cliff in Ireland, where it looks out over the Atlantic Ocean.

The discovery is in research published in Astronomy and Astrophysics titled "Euclid: Discovery of a quasar at z = 8.13 hosting a 360-million-solar-mass black hole." The lead author is Julien Wolf, who was a postdoc at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy when the research was done.

It has been revealed that one of the hallmarks of modern astronomy is the discovery of massive objects in the Universe that formed much sooner than astronomers thought they could. The JWST is driving much of this.

"Quasars powered by rapid accretion onto supermassive black holes (SMBHs) have been uncovered deep into the first gigayear of cosmic history," the authors write.

Recent findings suggest that now the Euclid Space Telescope is contributing to that trend. Euclid was rolled out to study dark energy and the expansion of the Universe. A big part of that job is measuring galaxies at different redshifts in its Euclid Wide Survey, to see how their morphologies are different over time. That will reveal how dark energy has changed over time.

This is what DÃºn Aonghasa, the new quasar, looks like in the actual Euclid image. It's the red dot in the center. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/J. Wolf et al.

Euclid found DÃºn Aonghasa in its Euclid Wide Survey imaging, but didn't confirm it. Follow-up observations by Keck, the Hubble, the Large Binocular Telescope, and especially the JWST provided the confirmation. JWST spectroscopy let the researchers measure "a systemic redshift of zsysâ=â8.129âÂ±â0.005, corresponding to only 630âMyr after the Major Bang and shifting the quasar redshift frontier by â39âMyr," the authors write. 39 million years is about 6% of the age of the Universe at that epoch. The quasar is now the first quasar observed at z > 8.

Recent findings suggest that DÃºn Aonghasa's luminosity is what lets astronomers observe it at such a great distance. Its luminosity helped researchers measure its mass and its accretion rate, and DÃºn Aonghasa contains 360 million solar masses.

This figure indicates absolute UV magnitude as a function of redshift for high-redshift quasars, galaxies, LRDs, LBDs, and other JWST-selected AGN up to zâ=â11. Orange squares show recently identified Euclid quasars, and the green star shows DÃºn Aonghasa, which is more UV-luminous than the LRDs, other JWST-selected AGN, and Lyman-break galaxies at comparable redshifts. JWST-selected AGN are shown as circles and colour-coded according to their phenomenological classification: LRDs in red, LBDs in blue, and other AGN in black. Previously known quasars are shown as grey circles. Open purple diamonds are Lyman-break galaxies. Image Credit: J. Wolf et al. A&A Volume 715, November 2026 A356.

DÃºn Aonghasa and its high redshift brethren pose the same familiar question: how did they get so large so quickly?

"Assembling a black hole of several hundred million solar masses within the first few hundred million years, despite its at the moment sub-Eddington accretion rate, requires either a massive seed or sustained, highly efficient early growth," the authors write.

While an actual answer to their growth is elusive, finding them helps constrain an eventual answer.

In a recent development, âFinding quasars at ever-increasing distances, at the edge of the observable universe, teaches us something about how the black holes in their centres grew,â said lead author Wolf in a press release. âThe closer to the Major Bang we find them, the faster their black holes must have grown or the more massive they must have been at birth â or both.â.

Aside from their puzzling masses, these quasars also open different windows or probes into aspects of the early Universe. They give astronomers long sightlines into the intergalactic medium, letting them study its opacity during reionization, and its metal enrichment.

The quasars also serve as probes of how matter was distributed. "Quasars further mark rare, highly biased peaks in the underlying matter distribution and therefore trace the densest regions of the early large-scale structure," the researchers write.

Sources indicate that on galactic scales, these high-redshift quasars are probes of how SMBH masses and the masses of their host galaxies co-evolved. Both masses tend to correlate, but there's no obvious reason why. AGN feedback could play a role, so could mergers, or a shared source of fuel for growth. But there's no certainty, so finding more high-redshift quasars may lead to an answer.

These things are all related, but the main result of finding these quasars is facing the questions posed by their high masses.

It has been revealed that finding these quasars and supermassive black holes is forcing astronomers to consider different explanations for how they grew so massive so quickly. One explanation is super-Eddington accretion, but DÃºn Aonghasa isn't accreting matter that rapidly. Another is massive seeds, but current formation models struggle to accommodate those. Another explanation is that quasars experienced super-Eddington accretion very early in the Universe, under very different conditions.

Heavy seeds could explain these quasars, but what could they be? Astrophysicists don't know, but some candidates are Direct-Collapse Black Holes, or maybe sequential runaway stellar collisions in extremely dense star clusters.

Another, more exotic and theoretical possibility for heavy seeds is primordial black holes (PBH). These are theorized to have formed in the very first moments in the Universe, when dense pockets of gas collapsed directly into black holes. With such an early head start, these PBH could've formed into heavy seeds without needing physics-breaking levels of accretion.

Primordial black holes are only hypothetical. If they're real, they could've formed by direct collapse of dense pockets of matter shortly after the Significant Bang. They could've acted as seeds for the very early, very massive SMBH found in the Epoch of Reionization. Image Credit: ESA/Hubble, N. Bartmann., CC BY-SA.

Luminous quasars like DÃºn Aonghasa are rare in the Epoch of Reionization. So far, there are only seven of them. The only path to an explanation for their masses is through more observations that find more of these ancient quasars, and hopefully ones even more distant.

Sources indicate that âAnd this may happen sooner than we think,â noted co-author Silvia Belladitta a scientist at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy. âThis highlights how promptly Euclid is expanding our census of the most distant quasars. Each fresh discovery brings us closer to understanding how supermassive black holes formed and grew in the early universe.â.

Industry observers note that "DÃºn Aonghasa establishes a fresh quasar redshift frontier as the first confirmed quasar at zâ>â8, providing a powerful new benchmark for early SMBH growth," the researchers write in their paper's conclusion. Its large mass reveals that it must have grown a lot before it was observed, but its bolometric luminosity contradicts that. So the mystery of massive early SMBH and their quasars is still a puzzle.

Researchers predicted that Euclid will find between 8â23 quasars at zâ>â8, so hopefully, more are on their way.

âIt is unclear how far back in time these supermassive black holes powering luminous quasars exist, but Euclid has a good chance of finding out what that limit is,â stated MPIA scientist and co-author Eduardo BaÃ±ados.

According to recent reports, it might seem like researchers are chasing a receding horizon, almost like a dog chasing its tail. They build better telescopes in hopes of finding answers to difficult questions. Then their telescopes uncover some answers, but also uncover more questions. It's probably true that there's no end to knowledge and we'll never know everything. But that also means there's no end to learning, no end to Nature, and no end to wonder.

Industry News: Intermittent Fasting May Not Work the Way Scientists Thought for Liver Health

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A clinical trial suggests that improving liver health may require less attention to strict fasting schedules and more emphasis on developing eating habits that people can sustain.
  • Sources indicate that for people using intermittent fasting to reduce fat in the liver, finding a meal schedule that helps them lose weight may be more important than eating at specific times of the day.
  • Led by the University of Granada (UGR) and the Public University of Navarra, the multicenter study was published in JHEP Reports and involved 197 adults aged 30 to 60 with overweight or obesity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A clinical trial suggests that improving liver health may require less attention to strict fasting schedules and more emphasis on developing eating habits that people can sustain.

Sources indicate that for people using intermittent fasting to reduce fat in the liver, finding a meal schedule that helps them lose weight may be more important than eating at specific times of the day. A fresh clinical trial found that people who lost at least 5% of their body weight experienced the greatest reductions in liver fat, with no clear advantage to eating earlier or later in the day.

Led by the University of Granada (UGR) and the Public University of Navarra, the multicenter study was published in JHEP Reports and involved 197 adults aged 30 to 60 with overweight or obesity. The research forms part of the doctoral dissertation of Antonio Clavero Jimeno, a predoctoral researcher at the University Joint Institute for Sport and Health (iMUDS) at UGR.

The researchers conducted a secondary analysis of a clinical trial previously published in Nature Medicine. That trial found that participants who practiced intermittent fasting lost an average of 3 to 4 kilograms (6.6 to 8.8 pounds) more than those who received only nutritional recommendations, regardless of their eating schedule. Eating earlier in the day, which in Spain often amounts to skipping dinner, also produced specific improvements in certain measures of blood sugar regulation.

To investigate whether these eating schedules offered additional benefits for liver health, the researchers compared three forms of time-restricted eating (TRE), a type of intermittent fasting that confines food consumption to specific hours of the day.

It has been revealed that participants were randomly assigned to four groups: standard care, early eating (approximately 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.), late eating (2 p.m. to 10 p.m.), and a self-selected eating window (12:20 p.m. to 8 p.m. on average). Over 12 weeks, all four groups received the same nutritional education program based on the Mediterranean diet and healthy lifestyle habits.

The researchers used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure liver fat and examined liver stiffness, liver enzymes, circulating proteins involved in liver metabolism, and other indicators of liver health.

Sources indicate that although liver fat decreased in all three intermittent fasting groups, none experienced statistically significant improvements beyond those achieved through standard care. The timing of meals also made no significant difference to other measures of liver health or the composition and diversity of microorganisms living in the gut.

Approximately 40 to 45% of participants practicing intermittent fasting lost at least 5% of their body weight. Reaching this threshold was associated with significantly greater reductions in liver fat, and most participants who achieved it belonged to the fasting groups. Greater reductions were also observed among people who already had hepatic steatosis, an excessive accumulation of fat in the liver, at the beginning of the study.

“The results do not suggest that intermittent fasting is ineffective, but rather that choosing an early, late, or self-selected fasting window does not appear to provide any additional benefit for liver health,” explain Manuel Dote Montero and Antonio Clavero Jimeno, the study’s first authors.

For the researchers, “the most notable factor seems to be choosing a strategy that facilitates clinically significant weight loss and can be sustained over time.”.

It has been revealed that references: “Time-restricted eating, liver health, and fecal microbiota in adults with overweight or obesity: A randomized controlled trial” by Manuel Dote-Montero, Antonio Clavero-Jimeno, Adrián Cortés-Martín, Amaya Lopez-Pascual, Elisa Merchán-Ramírez, Alba Camacho-Cardenosa, Mara Concepción, Maddi Osés, Alejandro López-Vázquez, Francisco J Amaro-Gahete, Juan J Martin-Olmedo, Lucas Jurado-Fasoli, Alejandro De-la-O, Patricia V García Pérez, Julio Gálvez, Alba Rodriguez-Nogales, Federico Garcia, Carmen Mbongo Habimana, Marcos Jiménez Vázquez, Víctor Manuel Alfaro-Magallanes, Matías A Avila, Jose L Martín-Rodríguez, Rafael Cabeza, Manuel Muñoz-Torres, Idoia Labayen and Jonatan R Ruiz, 7 July 2026, JHEP Reports. Some fish swimming in Montana’s Upper Missouri River today may have hatched before the 20th century began. Researchers have confirmed that blue suckers can live up to 130 years, more than three times their previously estimated lifespan of roughly 40 years. The discovery places the species among the longest-lived vertebrates in North America.

Industry observers note that the findings, published in Communications Biology, come from a study co-led by Alec Lackmann of the University of Minnesota Duluth, Luke Holmquist of Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks, and Allen Andrews of the University of Hawai’i at Mānoa. By examining microscopic structures inside the fishes’ heads and using a chemical signature left by nuclear weapons testing, the scientists uncovered evidence of extraordinary longevity and a population increasingly dominated by old individuals.

Recent findings suggest that the blue sucker (Cycleptus elongatus) is native to 23 U.S. states but is classified as imperiled in 22 of them. For decades, researchers monitoring the Upper Missouri River have observed increasingly large fish and remarkably few juveniles. The pattern suggests that young blue suckers have struggled to survive and join the adult population.

Sources indicate that “For decades, there has been conservation concern for the species across much of its range,” the researchers wrote. “Nonetheless, no validated age-based life history information exists for the species, which is a major knowledge gap.”.

According to recent reports, to investigate, the team collected and examined nearly 50 blue suckers between 2023 and 2026. More than 60 percent were older than 90 years, and some had survived for approximately 130 years. Their age distribution suggests that successful recruitment of new generations has become less frequent since major dams were installed in the mid-1900s. Habitat fragmentation associated with those dams is a possible contributor, although the study does not establish it as the cause.

The researchers determined the fishes’ ages by examining otoliths, tiny structures commonly called earstones that occur in approximately 97 percent of fish species. These structures grow throughout a fish’s life, accumulating annual layers that scientists can count under a microscope, much like the growth rings of a tree.

Blue suckers presented a technical challenge because their otoliths are exceptionally small. “Blue suckers have extremely small otoliths, smaller than the buffalofishes, but we figured out how to work with them,” Lackmann remarked.

As the researchers examined the growth layers, they encountered ages that far exceeded established expectations. In fish previously thought to live around four decades, “we were seeing the population had ages up to 130 years old,” Lackmann noted. “When age estimates are that much older than previously thought, an additional line of evidence is needed to rigorously test their validity.”.

To independently verify the ages, the team turned to bomb radiocarbon dating, a technique that uses the atmospheric changes caused by nuclear weapons testing during the Cold War. Those tests produced a distinctive increase in radioactive carbon-14 that became incorporated into living organisms, including the tissues of fish.

“Thermonuclear bombs that were tested in the mid to late 1950s and early 1960s more than doubled the amount of radiocarbon in the atmosphere,” said Lackmann.

Industry observers note that “This left a time-specific marker in organisms that lived through the bomb pulse. And if you’re able to quantify growth bands in an individual (for example, in trees, otoliths of bony fish, etc.) that is estimated to have lived through the bomb pulse, you can actually test to determine if the ages you are quantifying are accurate. Bomb radiocarbon dating is one of the best ways to age-validate long-lived organisms. So that’s where we have multiple lines of evidence here, otoliths providing the age estimates, and bomb radiocarbon confirming and validating the otolith ages and extreme longevity of the blue sucker.”.

By comparing the carbon-14 signatures in the otoliths with the known timing of the atmospheric radiocarbon increase, the researchers validated the ages estimated from the growth layers. This independent evidence confirmed that blue suckers can survive for more than a century.

According to recent reports, the blue sucker is now the fourth member of the sucker fish family (Catostomidae) found to reach 100 years or older, joining the bigmouth buffalo, smallmouth buffalo, and black buffalo. All four species have had their exceptional longevity documented since 2019, partly through advances in fish aging techniques.

Blue suckers also challenge expectations about how river environments shape animal lifespans. Unlike fish inhabiting relatively calm lakes, they spend their lives in fast-flowing rivers, where maintaining position and navigating currents can require considerable energy. Such environments have often been associated with faster life histories, making the species’ extreme longevity particularly unexpected.

The oldest fish examined had already been alive for decades when many of the dams now shaping the Missouri River system were constructed. Their survival across more than a century of environmental change contrasts with the apparent scarcity of younger generations, raising conservation concerns about whether aging adults are being replaced.

“To put a timeline on some of those older fish: the oldest one hatched around two years after Montana became a state, around the dawn of the automobile, like 20 years before the Titanic sank – it’s just wild,” said Holmquist.

“We start putting it in the context of what the landscape looked like when these fish hatched, and all the changes that have happened since—and they just keep swimming along in the river.”.

Reference: “Bomb-radiocarbon validated otoliths reveal 130-year lifespans and declining recruitment for blue sucker Cycleptus elongatus of the Upper Missouri River, Montana, USA” by Alec R. Lackmann, Allen H. Andrews, Luke M. Holmquist, Negar Haghipour, Grant Grisak, Molly A. H. Webb, Mark E. Clark and Zachary R. Shattuck, 18 November 2026, Communications Biology. DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-11219-3.

Universe Today's AI Policy

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, well, it's time to talk about everyone's favourite topic these days: artificial intelligence.
  • In a recent development, we won't be using AI to generate content on the site.
  • I proposal to pay humans to create Universe Today content until the robots make this career untenable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, well, it's time to talk about everyone's favourite topic these days: artificial intelligence. Specifically, what's our overall policy about it here at Universe Today?

In a recent development, we won't be using AI to generate content on the site. We won't write stories with AI, or make pictures, we won't make background music, and we won't generate video clips using AI.

I proposal to pay humans to create Universe Today content until the robots make this career untenable.

In a recent development, is that something you'd like to support? Join our https://patreon.com/universetoday and join the others who are keeping Universe Today independent and ad-free.

Join our Patreon. Support our work. Credit: Anton Podznyakov.

First, a preamble. My background is in computer science, and the tech nerd in me has been watching with fascination and excitement at the growing capabilities of the technology. I've built an incredible set of personal tools that help me manage the Universe Today website, organize our podcast catalog, transcribe interviews, and so much more. I'm starting to run out of ideas for things to build, which has never happened to me before.

Sources indicate that as a person who shares a planet with other humans, I'm concerned about a growing divide between those with access to technology and those without. I'm saddened by the training of LLMs on the work of artists without any compensation to mass produce competing work. I'm working overtime to patch up and harden computers that are getting shredded by automated hacking tools. I'm deeply concerned about our inability to control all this, and a seeming unwillingness to even bother by the people making this technology.

If you're building a machine that can destroy humanity... DON'T BUILD THE MACHINE. Seriously.

In a recent development, as a person who likes to watch stuff, play games, and read interesting stories, the Internet is starting to feel like a minefield. I'll start to watch a YouTube video and hear the telltale "it's not X it's Y," and realize that I'm just listening to an AI script. Creators I've been following for a decade have suddenly replaced their real, authentic presence with a script from Claude.

Sources indicate that it's heartbreaking, but it's understandable. The pressure growing to produce more content, faster, faster. And when everyone else is using AI, you'd have to be an idiot not to do the same.

I recently did a poll on my YouTube channel asking my audience how they feel about AI-generated videos. What would they do if they knew an excellent video was generated by AI? About 75% of you would stop watching, and about 25% would keep going. Humanity's collective response seems to be ambivalence.

It has been revealed that the result of our user poll. We asked you if you'd stop watching a video if you knew it was written by AI. Credit: Universe Today/YouTube.

The main problem right now (apart from the society-wrenching chaos of summoning the machine god), is that we don't know when something was written by AI and when it was done by a human. I know your AI detection skills are top notch and you'd never be fooled by an AI script, but I promise you... you have. And it's just going to get worse.

Industry observers note that I don't hate AI, sometimes, I love it. I especially miss the Will Smith Eats Spaghetti era when AI videos were like a cyberpunk fever dream. But I hate being lied to. I hate being deceived by someone who is presenting a video, or writing an essay, or sharing a heartfelt post on Reddit, implying that this is their actual opinion. But it's not, they outsourced it to an AI. I could just skip the middleman and ask the AI directly. "Dear Claude, please write me an essay about who would win in a fight, Batman or Wolverine. Now turn it into a video.".

Here's a video I recently did about how I feel about watching videos and discovering they're made with AI.

It has been revealed that the answer is disclosure. Just say what you did, so I don't have to check your work with Pangram and discover that 100% of your video script was written by AI.

And if you do disclose, then I and the other potential consumers of your content can decide for ourselves if we want to watch it, or read it, or listen to it. 25% will stick around, apparently.

Sources indicate that you're probably wondering at this point why the publisher of Universe Today is giving you his personal take on AI content. Why not just explain my policies, put it in the footer or something?

Because I'm human, I'm grieving, but I'm in a position to do something about it.

It has been revealed that universe Today is a space news website, written by humans, for humans. This means that humans chose our topics and story ideas, and humans did the reporting and writing to bring you the articles on the website. We don't use generative AI to produce articles, images, music or video clips on the website, in our podcasts or videos.

In a recent development, one caveat on images/videos. These are often provided by the original researchers or press office (et tu NASA?), and are sometimes made with a blend of AI and human artwork. We don't always spot it, but we replace the visuals when we do, or clearly identify them. If you think we got it wrong, [let us know].

Our words were written by humans, but quotes from researchers, or captions supplied by news sources might be written by AI. That's on them, we're not their Dad.

We may use AI coding assistance for internal development projects. We may also use AI tools for literature search, translation, transcription, grammar and spelling. We'll use AI to assist in researching a topic to better understand it, but it's only there to help a human make something better.

If we get something wrong, we'll fix it in the article and let you know what changed.

And we'll keep doing this until we go out of business, due to a lack of patrons, complete irrelevance, or the end of the world.

Join our https://patreon.com/universetoday to help make this a viable strategy for us.

The day we decided to remove all the advertising from Universe Today and be supported 100% by our patrons.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most prominent features on the Moon is one we canât regularly see, at least not completely. The South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin is one of the largest, oldest, and deepest impact craters on the Moon, and until recently weâve only been able to observe it from afar - and even then only when we sent orbiters around to the far side, which is never in direct line of sight with the Earth. Recently China has been busily sending landers and rovers to the site, and a new paper, published in Science Advances, details the actual samples returned to Earth by the Changâe-6 mission and combines them with the in-situ data from the Changâe-4 mission and rover. Those details combine to form a complete geological history of the major impacts that formed the basin, and some insight into the age of other impact craters scattered throughout the solar system.

It has been revealed that A sense of scale and time helps in understanding the SPA. Itâs roughly 2,200 kilometers across, making it similar in length to the north-south axis of mainland China. And it runs up to 10 kilometers deep, much deeper than any comparable land-based feature on Earth. For a long time, astronomers and planetary scientists have been debating how old it is, with dates ranging from 4.35 billion years ago to around 4.2 billion. That discrepancy is part of what the fresh paper hopes to solve, but thereâs another larger discrepancy it hopes to solve as well.

It has been revealed that the two halves of the Moon - the one that faces us and the one facing away - appear very different in terms of their features. The nearside is covered in smooth, dark plains called âmariaâ, whereas the far side has many more craters, with almost no volcanic plains and a thick layer of crust sitting on top. This difference, known as the âlunar dichotomy,â has stumped scientists for years. To solve it, many have turned to the SPA.

Fraser talks about collecting the Chang'e-6 moon rocks.

SPA was formed during a gigantic ancient collision that broke through the crust on the far side and exposed underground rock that had been buried since the Moonâs formation. But the main crater isnât the only one in the area. Various smaller craters have formed overlapping the main one, including the Von KÃ¡rmÃ¡n crater (where Changâe-4 landed with its Yutu-2 rover) and the 490-kilometer-wide Apollo basin, where Changâe-6 landed and that was created by a separate impact.

Crucially, those impacts created different types of magnesium-rich igneous rocks. One type, found by Changâe-4 in the Von KÃ¡rmÃ¡n crater, is known as moderately magnesium-rich norite. It crystallized directly from the vast sea of molten rock generated when the SPA-forming asteroid slammed into the Moon. Over millions of years, the lava lake this created cooled, and the minerals separated out into layers. Later impacts then pushed the solid rocks up to the peaks of newly formed craters, and eventually another impact known as the Finsen impact blasted pieces of that cooled lava lake into Von KÃ¡rmÃ¡n crater for Changâe-4 to find.

Sources indicate that another type of rock held even higher levels of magnesium. It was created via a process called magnesium-suite magmatism. When the SPA impact broke the Moonâs crust, the magma from its then liquid interior broke into the crust, cooling underneath its top layer. Later, the impact that created the Apollo basin pushed those now cooled materials up into its western peak ring, and then another impact that created whatâs now known as the Chaffee S crater blasted pieces of rock directly into the path of plains where Changâe-6 collected them billions of years later.

Fraser talks about the Chang'e-6 mission collecting lunar samples.

It has been revealed that combining the data from Changâe-4âs rover with data from around a gram of the 2kg returned by the Changâe-6 mission, while adding a sprinkle of computer simulations, the research team reconstructed a timeline of the early bombardment history of the Moon. The main feature was when SPA was created around 4.34 billion years ago, only a few hundred million years after the solar system itself formed.

The Apollo basin seemed to have been formed around 4.2 billion years ago, definitively answering why previous estimates of the SPA itself ranged from 4.35 billion years to 4.2 billion or so. Even later, around 3.87 billion years ago, another massive collision created what is now known as the Orientale basin, and after it came smaller impacts like Finsen and Chaffee S, which showered the entire region with debris that mixed the crust rocks in with the soil that formed on the Moon over hundreds of millions of years.

According to recent reports, while itâs great to know the Moonâs impact history, this research also has implications for other craters on other worlds. By counting them and using radiometry to estimate their ages, researchers can estimate when there were major swarms of asteroids impacting the inner solar system. In turn, that supplies potential evidence for the path the giant planets took during their early orbital history, feeding into a theory known as the Nice model.

But weâre not done with the lunar landscape yet. The SPA is a prime target for future crewed missions, and as more rovers, landers, and, potentially, people start to traverse the wilds of the lunar surface, theyâll occasionally come across fragments of the ancient crust created by massive impacts beyond anything our species has ever witnessed in the solar system. Itâs kind of cool to think that those fragments have been waiting billions of years for us to find and study them.

Bumblebees May Hold the Secret to How Intelligence Evolved

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (417 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bumblebees can solve unfamiliar problems, learn complex skills by watching others, and even transmit emotion-like states to their nestmates.
  • In a new Perspective published in Science, researchers Lars Chittka and Stanley Heinze examine growing evidence that advanced cognitive abilities may emerge through evolutionary modifications to ancient neural circuits.
  • In one experiment, bumblebees learned to move a ball and climb onto it to reach an otherwise inaccessible source of nectar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bumblebees can solve unfamiliar problems, learn complex skills by watching others, and even transmit emotion-like states to their nestmates. They accomplish all this with fewer than a million neurons, challenging the long-standing assumption that sophisticated intelligence requires a large brain.

In a new Perspective published in Science, researchers Lars Chittka and Stanley Heinze examine growing evidence that advanced cognitive abilities may emerge through evolutionary modifications to ancient neural circuits.

In one experiment, bumblebees learned to move a ball and climb onto it to reach an otherwise inaccessible source of nectar. They could even guide the ball toward a target that was no longer visible, suggesting an ability to mentally represent goals and solve unfamiliar problems.

Another study published in Nature found that bumblebees could learn to open a two-step puzzle box by observing trained nestmates, even though none independently discovered the solution.

Industry observers note that bumblebees also appear capable of transmitting emotion-like states. After receiving an unexpected reward, bees displayed an optimism-like bias when interpreting ambiguous stimuli. Other bees developed a similar bias simply by observing them through a transparent barrier, without physical contact or chemical communication.

“The remarkable cognitive abilities of bees may not have required them to evolve entirely new neural algorithms,” Chittka and Heinze write.

One possible explanation lies in the mushroom bodies, insect brain structures involved in learning and memory. Bumblebees possess approximately 50 times as many specialized neurons called Kenyon cells as fruit flies, giving them greater memory capacity. Additional circuits involved in navigation and decision-making may also allow bees to weigh multiple goals and plan their actions.

“More broadly, higher cognitive processes could have evolved many times and might be more widespread than previously thought,” the authors write.

Scientists have already produced a complete wiring diagram, known as a connectome, of the fruit fly brain. Similar efforts are underway in several bee species. Comparing these neural networks could reveal which evolutionary changes enable sophisticated cognition.

Sources indicate that “It seems likely that, just like between birds and mammals, different neural solutions might have evolved to produce similar cognitive traits in different insects,” write the authors. “Both shared and distinct solutions that shape the cognitive abilities of animals might emerge as general principles, and some might apply to both vertebrates and invertebrates.”.

It has been revealed that reference: “Bumble bee cognition” by Lars Chittka and Stanley Heinze, 19 November 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aek1724.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 9.5-million-year-old fossil discovery suggests that an ecological relationship observed in modern oceans has ancient origins.

A whale that sank to the bottom of an ancient sea approximately 9.5 million years ago may have attracted a community of marine scavengers. Scientists excavating fossil deposits in southern Denmark have discovered microscopic skeletal plates that belong to a previously unknown species of brittle star, a marine invertebrate closely related to starfish.

In a recent development, named Ophiura huebnerjenseni, the species may provide the earliest fossil evidence of brittle stars gathering around dead whales. Such carcasses create temporary ecosystems known as whale falls, supplying abundant food to organisms living on the seafloor. Brittle stars frequently inhabit these environments today, but their association with whale falls had never been documented in the fossil record.

It has been revealed that the remains were recovered from sediment collected during the 2018 excavation of a beaked whale’s lower jaw and several vertebrae at Denmark’s Gram Clay Pit. Researchers washed and sieved the sediment before examining individual microfossils using scanning electron microscopy. Subtle differences in the structure of the brittle stars’ skeletal plates allowed the team to identify a new species.

The distribution of the fossils suggested that their proximity to the whale was more than coincidental.

Industry observers note that “Only three samples taken directly beside the whale bones contained brittle-star remains. Samples from the same layer farther from the skeleton, and other comparison samples, yielded none,” the lead author Ben Thuy explains.

Sources indicate that the researchers investigated whether ocean currents or favorable fossil preservation conditions could explain the unusual concentration of skeletal plates. Fragments of sea urchins, which have similar physical and chemical properties, provided a useful comparison.

“We considered whether currents had simply concentrated the plates around the bones, or whether local chemical conditions had helped preserve them. However, sea-urchin fragments of comparable size and mineral composition occurred in every sample studied. This makes a preservation-only explanation less likely and supports the interpretation that the brittle stars lived on or close to the whale carcass,” Thuy added.

The Gram Clay Pit preserves sediments deposited beneath the ancient North Sea during the Late Miocene. Although the site has yielded numerous whale skeletons, exceptionally large megalodon vertebrae, and a diverse collection of marine invertebrates, brittle stars had previously escaped detection.

In a recent development, A decomposing whale delivers a substantial supply of organic material to the seabed. In modern oceans, whale falls can support successive communities of scavengers, opportunistic invertebrates, and, particularly in deep water, organisms sustained by chemical processes associated with decomposition.

Although the fossils cannot establish what Ophiura huebnerjenseni ate or whether it depended on whale carcasses, researchers suspect it was a generalist species that normally occupied the surrounding seabed and congregated where food became abundant.

“We interpret the site as a shallow-water whale fall at a stage when enrichment from the carcass supported opportunistic animals,” remarked Mette Elstrup. “We found no evidence for the later sulfide-based community stages that can develop at deep-sea whale falls. The discovery therefore adds a rare fossil perspective on how animals responded to a large food source on an ancient shallow-water seabed,” Elstrup said.

Sources indicate that the latest species takes its name from Holger Hübner and Thomas Jensen, founders of Germany’s Wacken Open Air heavy metal festival. The connection extends beyond the scientific tribute, however, to the geological origins of the festival’s famously muddy grounds.

Researchers believe the dark gray mud encountered by festivalgoers probably originates from the same geological deposits that preserved the ancient brittle stars.

“The clay that accumulated on the bottom of the ancient North Sea not only preserved the remains of a 9.5-million-years old brittle star, it also turns Wacken Open Air into the muddy battlefield renowned by metalheads worldwide,” concludes Lea Numberger-Thuy.

Reference: “A upcoming brittle star (Ophiuroidea, Ophiuridae) associated with a whale fall from the Miocene of Gram, Denmark” by Ben Thuy, Mette Elstrup, Lea D. Numberger-Thuy and Trine Sørensen, 19 October 2026, Neues Jahrbuch für Geologie und Paläontologie – Abhandlungen. DOI: 10.1127/njgpa/2026/1335.

Robots, Not Astronauts, Will Have to Fix Space Data Centers

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that yesterday we explored some of the difficulties facing orbital data centers in our look at the bottleneck of launching enough solar panels and radiative cooling systems to power the AI computing boom in space.
  • Recent findings suggest that modern hardware powering Artificial Intelligence even on Earth has an obsolescence problem.
  • Unfortunately, that means throwing away literal tons of still-useful solar panels and heat radiators just to discard some obsolete computer hardware.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that yesterday we explored some of the difficulties facing orbital data centers in our look at the bottleneck of launching enough solar panels and radiative cooling systems to power the AI computing boom in space. JPL physicist Dr. Slava Turyshev, who wrote the paper at the center of that article, also published a follow-up study in August, available in preprint on arXiv, about how getting the hardware off the ground is only half the battle. Once all that equipment is up there, someone, or something, is going to have to maintain it.

Recent findings suggest that modern hardware powering Artificial Intelligence even on Earth has an obsolescence problem. The computer chips and memory that power AI data centers become obsolete every 3-5 years. If a manufacturer builds an orbital data center, its processing power is effectively useless for training the latest AI models in less than half a decade. So, in their business looks, the solution is to build intentionally disposable satellites.

Unfortunately, that means throwing away literal tons of still-useful solar panels and heat radiators just to discard some obsolete computer hardware. Given that those bulkier pieces of equipment pose their own challenge for introduces, as we saw yesterday, that seems a bit of a waste. So, Dr. Turyshev suggests that orbital data centers must be designed with hardware replacement in mind.

Fraser talks about a NASA project designed to assemble large-scale structures in space.

On Earth, replacement of data server racks involves a human technician walking down an air-conditioned aisle, pulling some cables, and pressing pins before replacing a standardized blade. In orbit, that would require a pressurized housing with airlocks, life support and fire suppression systems, while still having the problem of cooling all of those heat-producing microchips in the vacuum of space. According to Dr. Turyshev, that means the entire data center architecture should be based around plug-and-play âorbital replacement unitsâ (ORUs).

Recent findings suggest that he assigns each of those ORUs into one of three main replaceable component tiers (alongside replacing an entire 100 kW satellite node if it suffers catastrophic damage). One is a 5 kW âcomputeâ module that holds the memory, storage and optical transceivers necessary to actually perform calculations. These are designed to be rapidly swappable, and are intended to be the most replaced part of the whole satellite.

In a recent development, another ORU category is the âsubsystemsâ â the power converters, batteries, pumps, and manifolds meant to keep the whole system running but that are settled enough technologically to not require regular replacement. In the paperâs architecture, these can be swapped out by specialized 6 or 7 degree-of-freedom robotic arms, as compared to the automated cartridge changers that handle replacing the compute modules.

Fraser talks about the difficulties repairing missions at L2, like JWST.

The third group of ORUs consists of the solar arrays and radiator panels themselves. Making them modular has the added advantage of not needing to replace the entire cooling or power generation system if one part happens to be struck by a micrometeoroid, which will undoubtedly happen often even in Low Earth Orbit. Despite the fact these modules make up the bulk of the weight and surface area of the spacecraft, they will not have to be repaired as frequently as the compute modules, as random failures caused by cosmic rays will brick compute modules fairly frequently..

It has been revealed that unfortunately, replacing these systems isnât as easy as it would be on Earth. Each 5 kW processor will heat up nearly half a degree Celsius every second, triggering a thermal overload in a little less than a minute if left uncooled. And the power capacitors riding along to maintain power to the system have the capability of producing an arc strong enough to weld a robotic gripper to a maintenance touch point, so they must be bled off before a robot can start interacting with the satelliteâs hardware.

It has been revealed that and then, there is once again the sense of scale. For a standardized 1 MW cluster, comprising ten 100 kW sized systems, a collection of 3-4 robots specialized assigned to each 1MW cluster would have to perform around four hundred standardized swaps per year â more than one a day. This would include replacing broken or damaged parts, as well as upgrading to the server hardware itself.

Recent findings suggest that hubble has already been repaired by a crewed mission. NASA wants to do it again, Great Space expliains. Credit - Great Space YouTube Channel.

According to recent reports, scaling that up once again to a 1 GW computer cluster, comparable to a major modern AI campus here on Earth, the number becomes staggering. There would have to be 400,000 automated replacement tasks every year. And supplying the parts to do that would require launching up to 25 metric tons of replacement cargo every day.

To put it bluntly, we donât have that kind of launch capacity yet. Nor would sending humans up help manage such a drastic workload. The paper estimates that housing and feeding a crew of 4-6 technicians to actively manage a data center constellation would require $500 million to $1.5 billion per year. Until we get to the scale of several hundred megawatts to a gigawatt-level system, that is not economically feasible.

Thatâs not to say we couldnât launch specialized crewed repair missions occasionally. But at the scales needed to make a dent in the AI infrastructure we have down here on Earth, it would be hard to keep up with the overall maintenance workload using humans. And unfortunately, the entire concept of maintenance is another area that the back-of-the-envelope calculations of the companies that want to build orbital data centers seem to ignore.

Recent findings suggest that their solution is simply to add some extra hardware to account for the inevitable damage/failure that comes with operating in space. While that might work for a little while, if the strategy is to have a long-term data center presence in orbit, it's better to design for at least the possibility of continual operation rather than burning up tens of thousands of satellites in fireballs across the world every year. It remains to be seen if that message will get across to the people designing these systems, though.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The same fundamental physics that holds atomic nuclei together may also help explain why the Universe is expanding at an accelerating rate.
  • Dark energy accounts for approximately 70 percent of the Universe’s total energy budget, yet its physical origin has remained unknown since scientists discovered cosmic acceleration nearly three decades ago.
  • According to recent reports, the proposed explanation centers on Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the theory describing the strong nuclear force that binds quarks inside protons and neutrons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The same fundamental physics that holds atomic nuclei together may also help explain why the Universe is expanding at an accelerating rate. Researchers at the University of British Columbia (UBC) and the University of Sheffield have developed a theoretical model that connects dark energy to the strong nuclear force, potentially explaining cosmic acceleration without introducing undiscovered particles or newly introduced fundamental fields.

Dark energy accounts for approximately 70 percent of the Universe’s total energy budget, yet its physical origin has remained unknown since scientists discovered cosmic acceleration nearly three decades ago. Many proposed explanations rely on hypothetical particles or fields that have never been detected. The latest research, published in The Astrophysical Journal, instead draws on established principles of the Standard Model of particle physics.

According to recent reports, the proposed explanation centers on Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the theory describing the strong nuclear force that binds quarks inside protons and neutrons. According to QCD, even apparently empty space contains quantum fields with complex properties. The researchers suggest that the vacuum’s underlying structure could produce a small energy shift as the Universe expands, potentially accounting for the acceleration observed across cosmic distances.

A key feature of the model involves the vacuum’s topological properties, which describe aspects of its quantum structure that can influence physics over large distances. The researchers propose that this structure responds to cosmic expansion in a way that generates an effective dark energy contribution through its interaction with gravity.

“Our theoretical framework suggests no new particles may be required at all,” claims Professor Ariel Zhitnitsky of UBC’s Department of Physics and Astronomy, whose earlier theoretical work provided the foundation for the study. “The characteristic energy scale predicted from the QCD vacuum and gravity comes out close to the observed dark-energy scale today without having to introduce an ad-hoc new field nor new parameter.”.

Rather than introducing an adjustable parameter to reproduce the observed strength of dark energy, the framework derives its characteristic energy scale from established physical constants.

“The most striking result is that the observed dark-energy scale emerges naturally from known physical constants, without the need for any additional fitting parameters,” claims UBC Professor Ludovic Van Waerbeke.

According to recent reports, the researchers also investigated whether the framework could reproduce measurements of the Universe’s expansion history. Using astronomical observations, including light from distant exploding stars (supernovae) and radiation left over from the early Universe, they found that the model performed comparably to standard cosmological models in fitting the data.

“The idea that the quantum vacuum as described by QCD could have the right properties to account for the accelerated expansion of the universe is very intriguing,” says Dong Ha Lee, a PhD researcher at the University of Sheffield and lead author of the paper.

The analysis also indicates that the framework can reproduce the changing dark energy behavior suggested by current cosmological observations. Unlike a simple cosmological constant, which maintains a constant energy density over time, evolving dark energy models allow that density to change as the Universe expands.

It has been revealed that “It raises the possibility that dark energy could be connected to the established theory of the strong nuclear force, without introducing newly introduced fundamental fields. Testing models based on this idea against cosmological data is an essential step. Our analysis demonstrates that such a model can reproduce the evolving dark energy behavior suggested by current observations. This motivates further theoretical work to better understand how the QCD vacuum responds to cosmic expansion and to develop predictions that can be tested with future observations.”.

Industry observers note that although the model agrees with existing astronomical measurements, that agreement does not establish that the QCD vacuum is responsible for dark energy. Further theoretical work is needed to clarify how its quantum structure interacts with cosmic expansion and whether the framework produces predictions that distinguish it from competing explanations.

The team prepares to refine its calculations and compare the results with upcoming observations from next-generation space telescopes. More precise measurements of how the Universe has expanded over billions of years could help determine whether dark energy is connected to the same quantum physics that governs matter inside atomic nuclei.

Reference: “Evolving Dark Energy Is Vacuum Energy After All” by Dong Ha Lee, Carsten van de Bruck, Eleonora Di Valentino, Ludovic Van Waerbeke and Ariel Zhitnitsky, 20 November 2026, The Astrophysical Journal. DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/aeb9cc.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers have detected titanium oxide in gas form for the first time around a young, massive star. The detection offers a rare glimpse into the very earliest stages of solar system formation, before the formation of planets and asteroids.

In a recent development, the detection was made around a young protostar called Orion Source I, which lies some 1500 light-years from Earth. Orion Source I has not yet reached the main sequence phase of a starâs life cycle â it continues to accrete material from its surrounding molecular cloud.

According to recent reports, models of solar system formation have long held that certain rocky molecules, ones which are stable at high temperatures, act as the âseedsâ that make up the dust in a protoplanetary disk, and later form the basis for rocky planets like Earth and Mars. This includes elements like calcium, aluminum, and titanium. Only later do materials that vaporize easily â volatiles like water, for example â accrete to young solar system objects.

But itâs not exactly clear where these seeds form. Samples collected from our own solar system suggest that they form under high-temperature conditions. They are, as far as we can tell, the oldest solids ever formed in our solar system.

Now, for the first time, this detection of titanium oxide around Orion Source I is providing astronomers more direct evidence of vaporized rock at the dawn of a newly introduced star system.

âWe're in a unique situation with this object, Orion Source I,â noted Adam Ginsburg, Associate Professor at the University of Florida and a co-author on the paper announcing the discovery. âThis object has a luminous enough star that it's evaporating the rock. We're seeing the rock evaporate from solid into gas, and so we can do the spectroscopy now and figure out what the rock is made of.â.

Ginsberg and his coauthors are getting the first real glimpses at the formation environments of these rocky dust-seeding materials, which complements knowledge gathered from our own solar system.

Industry observers note that âThe exciting thing is we're seeing the titanium oxide; we can measure how much there is, and we can start comparing our measurements to how our own solar system formed,â Ginsburg stated. âIn our solar system, we can measure the ratios between different types of rocks, different elements, because we can grab those rocks and bring them into a lab.â.

This isnât the first time Orion Source I has provided valuable insights into solar system formation. In 2019, salty compounds were similarly detected in the protoplanetary disk.

In a recent development, while the salt was found mainly in the outer disk around the star, the titanium oxide was found closer in, at the base of the starâs outflow of material: a hotter, more extreme region where the material could be vaporized. Understanding the origin of this material is an important discovery for researchers trying to piece together exactly how a new solar system comes together, and offers a glimpse into the past of our own star and rocky neighbourhood.

The detection was published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters in 2026.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Successful potato harvests in simulated lunar soil suggest that future astronauts could recycle their food scraps to help grow their next meal.
  • Industry observers note that A future in which humans live on the Moon and grow their own food may be a little closer to reality thanks to one of Earth’s most familiar crops.
  • The findings support NASA’s Artemis program, which aims to establish a sustained human presence on the Moon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Successful potato harvests in simulated lunar soil suggest that future astronauts could recycle their food scraps to help grow their next meal.

Industry observers note that A future in which humans live on the Moon and grow their own food may be a little closer to reality thanks to one of Earth’s most familiar crops. Researchers at Oregon State University have successfully grown edible potatoes in simulated lunar soil, achieving growth and yields comparable to those produced on Earth by adding compost made with the help of earthworms.

The findings support NASA’s Artemis program, which aims to establish a sustained human presence on the Moon. Producing food locally would reduce dependence on costly resupply missions from Earth and help make long-term lunar exploration more sustainable. Potatoes are particularly appealing because they provide substantial nutritional value and produce more calories per unit of land than many other crops.

According to recent reports, “We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,” mentioned Aymeric Goyer of Oregon State University’s Department of Botany and Plant Pathology. “That’s an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.”.

One of the biggest agricultural challenges on the Moon lies directly beneath astronauts’ feet. Most of the lunar surface is covered in regolith, a layer of loose rock and dust containing very little organic matter.

In a study published in npj Microgravity, Goyer and his colleagues tested whether adding different amounts of vermicompost, a nutrient-rich material produced when earthworms break down organic matter, could make simulated lunar soil suitable for growing potatoes.

Because the composition of lunar regolith varies across the Moon, the team tested five simulants representing both the Moon’s darker plains, known as lunar maria, and its highland regions. For comparison, they included soil from Hermiston, Oregon, a region known for producing some of the highest potato yields in the world.

Potato plants grown in simulated lunar soil without compost were severely stunted and developed poorly formed roots. Adding between 5% and 15% vermicompost led to only partial recovery. However, plants grown with 30% vermicompost matched the growth and development of those cultivated in Earth soils.

Lunar regolith also contains elevated levels of heavy metals that can damage plant roots and interfere with growth.

“We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds,” stated David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer’s lab.

The researchers suspect that organic matter binds to heavy metals, making them less available to plants and limiting their harmful effects.

Growing potatoes successfully would mean little if astronauts could not safely eat them. Encouragingly, potatoes produced in the lunar soil simulants maintained their nutritional quality and demonstrated no statistically significant increase in glycoalkaloids, naturally occurring potato toxins often associated with green discoloration beneath the skin. The findings indicate that the potatoes were safe to eat under the conditions tested.

According to recent reports, future lunar explorers could potentially bring a small supply of organic matter from Earth and gradually produce more by recycling food scraps and plant waste. Such a system could turn everyday waste into valuable growing material while reducing the supplies astronauts would need to transport from Earth.

Sources indicate that the research team is now investigating which potatoes might be best suited for lunar agriculture. A forthcoming paper will report results from experiments involving 10 potato varieties grown in simulated lunar soil.

In a recent development, reference: “Growth and molecular responses of potato to lunar regolith simulants” by David Handy, Anika Loeffler, Medora Knudson, Sydney Campbell, Pankaj Jaiswal, Jeffrey C. Anderson and Aymeric Goyer, 19 November 2026, npj Microgravity. DOI: 10.1038/s41526-026-00668-z.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In an impressive technological maneuver, astronomers have harnessed three different supercomputers together to simulate the Milky Way at a level of detail never before achieved.
  • These results are in a paper titled "Architecture-Agnostic Exascale Star-by-Star Simulation of Our Galaxy," from the SC26: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the early days, astronomers kept sketchbooks close at hand when they looked through their telescopes. They drew what they saw and shared their drawings. Modern astronomy, with its enormous segmented lenses, gigabyte cameras, and cryogenically-cooled infrared space observatories, makes those days seem more distant than they really are. But one of the latest efforts in astronomy makes astronomy's sketch-pad days seem so far in the past, they're almost red-shifted.

In an impressive technological maneuver, astronomers have harnessed three different supercomputers together to simulate the Milky Way at a level of detail never before achieved. They used the supercomputers and AI together to simulate the Milky Way down to the level of individual stars. Up until now, the smallest level of detail in simulations, called particles, was clusters of stars with the mass of about 100 Suns. The behaviour of individual stars was averaged out in those simulations (Auriga, FIRE, etc.).

These results are in a paper titled "Architecture-Agnostic Exascale Star-by-Star Simulation of Our Galaxy," from the SC26: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis. The lead author is Keiya Hirashima, from RIKEN in Japan.

In simulations, achieving a level of individual stars means that individually simulated particles have one solar mass. So it's like a proxy for the population of stars. But regardless of that important distinction, the latest simulations are extraordinary.

"Our highest-resolution Milky Way simulation used 5.4 trillion particles, â¼ 10, 000Ã those in the state-of-the-art simulations," the authors write.

Industry observers note that âWe expect better simulations as computational power increases, but this still requires work on improving resolutions, and for a Milky Way-sized galaxy, itâs not straightforward,â said Professor Michiko Fujii from the Department of Astronomy at the University of Tokyo. âWhen we look at smaller regions in detail, we encounter areas where the gas is denser and changes rapidly. This means the simulation needs to take much shorter steps in time, which greatly increases the amount of calculation required.".

This figure from the paper shows different structures of disk galaxies at different scales, emphasizing the complexity necessary for accurate simulations. Top left and middle: NGC 4414, a disk galaxy similar to the Milky Way Galaxy, taken with the Hubble Space Telescope. Top right: NGC628, a disk galaxy with spiral arms and bubble structures taken with the JWST. Bottom left: Carina star forming region taken with the JWST. Bottom middle: Cassiopeia A supernova remnant taken with the JWST. Bottom right: turbulent innterstellar gas around Cassiopeia A taken with Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer. Image Credit: Hirashima et al. 2026. SC2026.

To achieve this fine particle resolution, simulations need ever shorter time steps, and time steps are like simulation currency; the shorter they are, the more computing resources they demand. To supply the resources for that, the researchers harnessed the power of three exascale supercomputers together: Aurora, Frontier, and JUPITER. Each one ran the same software on different hardware: Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD graphic processing units (GPUs) and central processing units (CPUs).

But linking three supercomputers was only part of the solution.

Industry observers note that "We overcame this problem by using an AI model to predict how gas around supernova explosions evolves," mentioned Fujii. "This allowed us to carry out the simulation more efficiently and achieve a level of detail where individual stars can be represented.".

By using this model, the larger simulation was able to skip over many small timesteps. It's called PHEASANT, and it was developed by postdoctoral researcher Keiya Hirashima from RIKEN. Supernovae are complex and require their own detailed simulations with very small timesteps. By plugging PHEASANT into the larger simulation, it relieved that simulation of a lot of work.

Recent findings suggest that "With trillions of particles, we resolve individual stars and model their SN feedback self-consistently within a galactic-scale simulation," the authors write. "Such a simulation reveals how individual stars, such as the Sun, contribute to the overall structure of the MW through multiple physical processes.".

Industry observers note that this image from PHEASANT highlights the Milky Way's disk. Galaxies are complex structures, with different types of structures at different scales. They have thin and thick disks, bulges, halos, spiral arms, star clusters, nebulae, and individual stars and gas clouds. In this work, the researchers divided the galaxy into smaller regions that could be processed by different parts of a supercomputer. Â©2026 PHEASANT/Hirashima/Fujii CC-BY-ND.

âOne of my parts was to develop an AI model that predicts how the gas surrounding a supernova explosion changes over time. If we calculate this process directly, we need time steps of around 100 years,â said Hirashima. âMy model predicts gas distribution after 100,000 years. This means that, rather than having to calculate every small step, we can use a much longer time step for the entire galaxy simulation. Making this work efficiently on different supercomputers was a challenge because each system uses different AMD, Intel, or NVIDIA CPUs and GPUs. Achieving good performance across all three systems required some specific optimizations.â.

In a recent development, these panels are snapshots from PHEASANT. The panel on the left shows the distribution and temperature of gas across a model galaxy. The panel on the right is a close-up view, where individual stars are visible as dots. Image Credit: Â©2026 PHEASANT/Hirashima/Fujii CC-BY-ND.

We can't understand the Milky Way, or galaxies in general, without a detailed understanding of how its gas and stars behave. Stars are born, drift away from their clusters, and evolve. Depending on their masses, they can remain on the main sequence for trillions of years, leave the main sequence after a few billion years and then linger as white dwarf cinders, or exhaust their fuel rapidly and explode as supernovae.

Sources indicate that gas is also complex. It collects in clouds where stars form, can be funnelled into the galactic center and "recycled" by supermassive black holes, or blasted away by explosions. Stars and gas are linked, and there's an extraordinary amount of detail involved.

Sources indicate that supernovae are among the most complicated events. In some regions, the massive young stars that eventually explode as supernova are born in the same region. When they exhaust their fuel, they explode and carve massive bubbles in the interstellar medium. That can drive gas away to form more latest stars elsewhere. They can even propel gas outside of the galaxy. It's all part of the life of the Milky Way, and simulations that struggle to recreate all of the detail in supernova explosions can lead astronomers astray.

This is LHA 120-N44 (N44) in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the ESO's Very Large Telescope. It features a massive bubble excavated in the interstellar medium by exploding young stars in its center. Some of the stars are still there, and they're still expanding the bubble with their powerful winds. Simulating all of the complexity involved is an enormous challenge. Image Credit: ESO/Manu Mejias.

According to recent reports, âSomething we want to understand is how events on the scale of individual stars connect to the larger structure of the Milky Way,â stated Fujii. âWith this simulation, we can investigate how individual supernovae affect the number of stars that form, the size of these giant gas bubbles and the material that flows out of the galaxy. We can also study how groups of stars form and how they may eventually develop into star clusters.â.

The PHEASANT AI surrogate model plays a critical role in this work, and that's part of a broader trend in science.

"The surrogate modeling approach can also be generalized beyond astrophysical problems to other research fields," the authors write.

"AI surrogate modeling accelerates simulations and bridges wider physical scales, opening new pathways in various real-world applications, including climate modeling, space forecasting, and low-temperature plasma," the authors conclude.
