A remote island in Upcoming Zealand was supposed to be a safe haven for wildlife

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A remote island off New Zealand’s coast reveals the challenges of protecting native birds from invasive predators.
  • Today’s Image of the Day from NASA Earth Observatory features Resolution Island, a remote expanse of wilderness off the southwestern coast of Latest Zealand.
  • Surrounded by deep blue waters and covered in dense vegetation, the island appears to be an ideal sanctuary for wildlife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A remote island off New Zealand’s coast reveals the challenges of protecting native birds from invasive predators.

Today’s Image of the Day from NASA Earth Observatory features Resolution Island, a remote expanse of wilderness off the southwestern coast of Latest Zealand.

Surrounded by deep blue waters and covered in dense vegetation, the island appears to be an ideal sanctuary for wildlife.

Its isolation, however, has not always offered the protection that conservationists envisioned.

For more than a century, Resolution Island has been at the center of an ambitious effort to preserve some of Latest Zealand’s most extraordinary native birds.

Its history reveals both the potential and the limitations of using islands as natural barriers against invasive species.

The image was captured on December 12, 2025, by the Operational Land Imager aboard the Landsat 9 satellite.

Resolution Island lies within Fiordland National Park, a spectacular region of mountains, forests, waterfalls, and narrow waterways that extend deep into the southwestern coast of New Zealand’s South Island.

During past ice ages, enormous glaciers moved through the region, gradually carving deep valleys into the landscape.

As the glaciers retreated and sea levels rose, ocean water flooded many of these valleys, creating the dramatic fjords visible today.

It has been revealed that resolution Island is the largest island within the national park. Its mountainous terrain reaches an elevation of 3,507 feet at the summit of Mount Clerke.

The island’s varied landscape supports wetlands, ancient evergreen forests, and high-elevation grasslands. These distinct environments provide a range of habitats for native wildlife.

New Zealand’s long geographical isolation allowed wildlife to evolve in remarkable ways.

Before humans arrived, the country had virtually no native land mammals other than bats. Birds occupied many ecological niches that mammals filled elsewhere in the world.

Some species gradually lost the ability to fly, while others developed behaviors that left them particularly vulnerable to ground-dwelling predators.

Among them were kiwi, which forage along the forest floor, and kākāpō, the world’s only flightless parrot.

For millions of years, these birds survived without facing the kinds of mammalian predators found on other continents.

That evolutionary advantage became a liability when people introduced unfamiliar animals into Latest Zealand’s ecosystems.

Rats, cats, and members of the weasel family brought newly introduced pressures that native birds were poorly equipped to withstand.

By the nineteenth century, the decline of Upcoming Zealand’s native wildlife was becoming increasingly apparent.

Industry observers note that european settlers had introduced stoats and other predators in an attempt to control rabbit populations. Instead, these animals created another ecological problem by preying on vulnerable native species.

In 1872, conservationist Thomas Henry Potts suggested that Resolution Island could provide a refuge for birds threatened by introduced predators.

The surrounding ocean appeared to offer a natural protective barrier, allowing native species to survive without the dangers they faced on the mainland.

Resolution Island became a protected reserve in 1891, making it part of a pioneering chapter in Latest Zealand’s conservation history.

Long before modern wildlife restoration programs existed, naturalists were experimenting with ideas that would eventually become central to endangered species management.

One of the most dedicated figures in this undertaking was Richard Henry, who became the island’s caretaker.

Henry recognized the urgency of protecting birds that were rapidly disappearing from other parts of the country.

Working in an isolated and physically demanding environment, he transported hundreds of native birds across the waters of Fiordland.

More than 700 birds, primarily kiwi and kākāpō, were relocated to Resolution Island and neighboring islands during his conservation efforts.

Much of the work involved traveling by rowboat through a region known for challenging weather and rugged terrain.

Henry’s efforts represented an early attempt to prevent extinction by establishing wildlife populations in geographically isolated locations.

Unfortunately, the assumption that the surrounding waters would keep predators away proved incorrect.

In a recent development, by 1900, invasive predators had been detected on Resolution Island. Stoats were capable of swimming across the channels that separated the island from nearby land.

The discovery undermined years of painstaking conservation work and exposed a weakness in the island’s natural defenses.

Sources indicate that stoats are highly adaptable hunters. Their ability to exploit different environments makes them particularly problematic in Fresh Zealand, where many native birds nest on or near the ground.

Henry attempted to control the invading predators through trapping but eventually left the island to pursue conservation work elsewhere.

His experience demonstrated that geographical isolation alone was not necessarily enough to protect vulnerable species.

More than a century later, conservationists continue to build on Henry’s original vision.

In 2008, Upcoming Zealand’s Department of Conservation launched a predator management program on Resolution Island to improve the prospects of native wildlife.

Maintaining such a program across a large, mountainous island presents considerable challenges.

Dense forests, steep slopes, and remote locations complicate efforts to monitor wildlife and control invasive animals.

Conservation also extends into the surrounding waters, where a marine reserve protects coastal ecosystems near the island’s distinctive Five Fingers Peninsula.

Viewed from space, Resolution Island offers a striking portrait of an apparently untouched wilderness.

Yet beneath its forest canopy lies a complex ecological history shaped by human intervention, invasive species, and generations of conservation work.

The island remains a powerful reminder that protecting nature sometimes requires far more than simply setting it aside.

An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • It has been revealed that in parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready.
  • In a recent development, what is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that in parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

In a recent development, what is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

In a recent development, californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

In a recent development, state officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, says environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

Recent findings suggest that in 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a big, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier says. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”.

It has been revealed that that waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she says. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this upcoming climate normal.

It has been revealed that 1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

But the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

Recent findings suggest that in 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

Not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” states Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

According to recent reports, but there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto says. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

Recent findings suggest that el Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, says Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento. And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

The El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

Sources indicate that as much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

Recent findings suggest that on February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

According to recent reports, “We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves says now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

“We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves said. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

The neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves notes. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

In a recent development, gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

In a recent development, he reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves says.

Recent findings suggest that the havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier says. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”.

Much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk glitch,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report said.

California’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier says. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

Those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

Recent findings suggest that such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a massive boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

It’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

Months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

In California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, says Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

In a recent development, as prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis says, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

Then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

Sources indicate that those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

Industry observers note that segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, indicates she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

Industry observers note that “Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she says. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”.

Industry observers note that but, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”.

What makes a hug truly memorable has a lot to do with empathy and how you handle relationships

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A survey of 15,049 adults demonstrates most people remember hugs for comfort and support.
  • We tend to think of a hug as a universal source of warmth, yet nearly three in ten adults in a large survey could not recall one that had left a positive mark.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A survey of 15,049 adults demonstrates most people remember hugs for comfort and support. Empathy, attachment patterns, and hugging habits also play a role.

We tend to think of a hug as a universal source of warmth, yet nearly three in ten adults in a large survey could not recall one that had left a positive mark.

When a hug did stick in someone’s memory, it was much more likely to be for comfort, support, or understanding than for romance.

Recent findings suggest that whether someone could remember a hug at all came down to a few key traits. The top three were how much empathy they felt, how they handled closeness, and whether they usually hugged their friends hello.

According to recent reports, anna Lena Dueren of the University of Bristol‘s School of Psychological Science led the analysis of 15,049 adults in the U.K. Their answers came from the Touch Test, a national survey on touch that BBC Radio 4 promoted in early 2020.

It has been revealed that the study is a snapshot of who remembers what. It can show which traits go together with a hug memory, not what causes one.

In an interview with Earth.com, Dueren put the main finding simply. “Most participants remembered hugs because they conveyed comfort, understanding, or support,” she mentioned.

To her knowledge, she added, it’s the first large study to ask people why a hug stayed with them.

The question was plain: is there a hug you remember because of its positive emotional effect on you? Of the 15,046 people who answered, 10,457 said yes, or 69.5 percent.

It has been revealed that people who mentioned yes then picked the single best reason from a short list. Among the 9,703 who chose a listed reason, about a third picked comfort, 29 percent said the hug conveyed understanding, and 20 percent said support.

Industry observers note that comfort, understanding, and support together cover more than four in five of the hugs people kept. Just 147 people, or 1.5 percent of the group, mentioned the hug was memorable because it was physically arousing.

Earlier studies had linked daily hugs to lower stress and better mood, and these answers fit.

Men and women were about equally likely to remember a hug at all. The reasons they gave, though, differed in a small but consistent way.

Among men, 3.9 percent chose arousal as the reason, compared with 0.8 percent of women. Men were also more likely to pick friendliness, 12.3 percent, in comparison to 4.8 percent of women.

It has been revealed that women chose comfort more often, at 34.6 percent to men’s 25.3 percent, and understanding more often too. The team suggested that the nurturing side of a hug may count for more among women.

Dueren’s team noted that only 2,197 men gave a reason, against 7,506 women, so they advise reading the gender differences with caution.

Dueren’s team, which includes researchers at UCL, the University of Sussex, and the University of Greenwich, then checked which traits went with keeping an emotional memory of a hug.

The strongest link was a habit: people who always greet friends and family with a hug were more likely to recall one.

Sources indicate that disliking the feel of being hugged went the other way, and so did finding it hard to know how firmly to hug someone. Asked by Earth.com what someone who dislikes hugging might take from the work, Dueren pointed to the size of the gap.

Sources indicate that “In our study, people who disliked the feeling of being hugged were slightly less likely to recall a hug that had a positive emotional effect on them than those who did not dislike it,” she remarked. “The findings highlight that hugging experiences are not equally remembered by everyone.”.

It has been revealed that empathy mattered too, whether measured as reading other people’s feelings or as feeling them alongside someone. Higher scores went with higher odds of remembering a hug.

So did attachment style, how a person relates to those closest to them. Insecure attachment comes in two forms.

People who feel distress at separation, the anxious form, were more likely to hold a hug in memory. People who prize independence in relationships, the avoidant form, were less likely to.

All of these effects were small, and together the traits explained only 10 to 14 percent of the variation in who remembered a hug.

Sources indicate that dueren’s team expected that people who are less satisfied with their bodies would be more likely to remember a hug for the comfort or support it gave. That expectation failed.

It has been revealed that A person’s satisfaction with their own body did not influence whether they remembered a hug, or why. However, there was a measure that did.

Industry observers note that the team built a five-item scale of how much a person’s sense of their body runs through touch. One item asked whether they choose clothes partly for how the fabric feels on the skin.

Recent findings suggest that people who scored higher on it were more likely to remember a hug, and to remember it for understanding or arousal rather than comfort. The scale is newly introduced, and the team called those results preliminary.

Being tucked in with a hug and a kiss as a child had no bearing on whether a person remembered a hug. Neither did how often that person gets hugged day to day.

In a recent development, the people who answered chose to take part and were not paid, so they may care about touch more than average. Three-quarters were women, and all lived in the U.K., where attitudes to touch differ from those elsewhere.

The survey didn’t ask who gave the remembered hug or where it happened, so it can’t say whether comfort from a partner is remembered differently from comfort given by a friend.

According to recent reports, answers were collected between January and March 2020, and fewer than 1 percent arrived after the U.K.’s first lockdown began. So this is a record of hugging before the pandemic changed it.

Dueren told Earth.com that she wants to pursue why the same hug feels so different to different people. “The same type of touch can feel pleasant for one person and uncomfortable to another,” she stated. “I would like to better understand factors that contribute to these differences in experience.”.

According to recent reports, empathetic people may store up hugs, or memorable hugs may make people more empathetic, and this survey can’t tell which. Settling that would mean following the same people over years, and that study has not yet been run.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS One.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day.
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.
  • The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

“Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”.

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

It has been revealed that before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

Industry observers note that “This has never been anything against John Thune,” remarked Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”.

Industry observers note that “Part of the issue here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Industry observers note that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

Sources indicate that but no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., noted voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

Sources indicate that “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul said.

Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

“Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they said, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Industry observers note that moreno mentioned, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”.

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., noted on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”.

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides said.

“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

Recent findings suggest that that long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune said he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”.

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

According to recent reports, “If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”.

#158682. Millions of Americans use a form of birth control that surveys have overlooked

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1442 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Millions of Americans use a form of birth control that surveys have overlooked

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1442 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More Americans use menstrual cycle tracking to avoid pregnancy than surveys suggested, with use rising in some states.
  • Tracking the menstrual cycle to avoid pregnancy may be far more common than scientists once believed.
  • Recent findings suggest that around 7% to 8% of US birth control people aged 18 to 44 tracked their cycles in 2022 and 2023.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More Americans use menstrual cycle tracking to avoid pregnancy than surveys suggested, with use rising in some states.

Tracking the menstrual cycle to avoid pregnancy may be far more common than scientists once believed. Based on national surveys conducted over the years, only a small share of Americans were thought to rely on it.

A fresh study tells a different story.

Recent findings suggest that around 7% to 8% of US birth control people aged 18 to 44 tracked their cycles in 2022 and 2023. That share nearly doubled by 2026 in three Western states.

Its popularity has also been underestimated because of the way most surveys count birth control people.

The study was led by Chelsea Polis, a principal research scientist at the Guttmacher Institute.

She worked with Rebecca Simmons, a research associate professor of obstetrics and gynecology at University of Utah Health.

No latest information was gathered for the project. Data from four large surveys were reanalyzed instead.

Cycle tracking for pregnancy prevention falls under a category of contraception known as fertility awareness-based methods (FABMs).

“I hope that these results are a shock to the family planning community,” Simmons remarked.

“There’s been a lot more acceptance of FABMs as legitimate methods over time, but most people still aren’t putting them on their radar enough for how important they are in the cultural milieu.”.

“This is a really key thing that I’m hoping that people will sit up and pay attention to right now.”.

Pregnancy is possible on only six to nine days of each menstrual cycle. These days fall around ovulation, when an egg is released by an ovary.

According to recent reports, some people count days on a calendar to work out when they are fertile. Others check their temperature every morning, and some watch for changes in cervical mucus. A smartphone app is used by some.

According to recent reports, to avoid pregnancy, they skip sex on fertile days or use condoms as a backup. People who are trying to conceive can use the same information.

More than a dozen fertility awareness-based methods exist, but they don’t all work equally well.

“FABMs are a method class,” Simmons mentioned.

“They’re not a single method. Within that method class, some of those methods, like the rhythm method, are not very effective, and some are actually comparable to the effectiveness of short-acting methods like pills or patches.”.

Sources indicate that two of the surveys covered the whole country. One was the 2022–2023 National Survey of Family Growth. The other was a 2022 survey on access to birth control.

The other two were limited to six states between them. One was conducted in Arizona, Newly introduced Jersey and Wisconsin. The Mountain West Sexual and Reproductive Health Survey was carried out in Idaho, Nevada and Utah.

Recent findings suggest that each survey recruited its participants in its own way. The time frame for current use also varied from the month of the interview to the previous three months.

Despite these differences, the four estimates for 2022 and 2023 fell within a narrow band of 6.6% to 8.3%.

The federal survey alone suggests that more than 2.2 million people in the US use these methods.

“Fertility awareness-based methods are used by a meaningful share of US contraceptive users,” Polis stated.

“Although many clinicians do not receive robust training on FABMs, our data show that FABMs are more frequently used than several other contraceptive methods that clinicians are routinely trained to provide.”.

Industry observers note that gaps in knowledge about birth control are nothing new. Earlier research found that many healthcare providers don’t offer self-injected birth control either.

Recent findings suggest that picture a woman who keeps track of her cycle and relies on condoms during her fertile days. A national survey would most likely record her as a condom user.

That happens because each person is usually assigned the most effective method they mention. Cycle tracking is ranked low on that scale and is therefore easily missed.

Such combined consumers made up about a quarter of cycle trackers in three surveys. In the fourth, they were close to half.

When they were added back into the federal survey, the estimate went from 4.3% to 6.6%. The standard approach had overlooked about a third of the people who track their cycles.

People who paired tracking with the pill, an IUD, an implant or sterilization were not counted. They accounted for about one in five cycle trackers, compared with roughly 9% in a 2013 to 2015 analysis.

In a recent development, several of those methods prevent ovulation entirely. In that case tracking offers almost no extra protection, and the researchers suggested that some users may not realize it.

Cycle tracking appears to be gaining ground, at least in some parts of the country.

Between 2019–2020 and 2022–2023, its use in Arizona, Fresh Jersey and Wisconsin increased from 5% to 6.9%.

Sources indicate that A sharper rise was recorded in Idaho, Nevada and Utah. There, the share of birth control customers who tracked their cycles stood at 7.5% in December 2022. It had grown to 12.5% by June 2024 and then to 14.5% by January 2026.

Sources indicate that most of this growth came in the first 18 months. The later increase was small enough that it could have been due to chance.

According to recent reports, is the same trend playing out nationwide? That question can’t be answered yet. Because the federal survey has since been redesigned, its latest results cannot be compared reliably with earlier rounds.

According to recent reports, several factors could be involved, according to Simmons. Concerns about hormonal birth control may be one.

It has been revealed that the popularity of tracking apps and difficulty getting other contraceptives may be others. None of these reasons was examined in the study.

Social media could be adding to the trend as well. Earlier studies of popular TikTok videos about birth control found cycle tracking was discussed more than any other method.

Among cycle trackers in the federal survey, 63% were married. Only 45% of people using other methods were.

The gap in Arizona, Fresh Jersey and Wisconsin looked much the same, at 60% versus 43%.

Cycle tracking only works when both partners cooperate. Couples in steady relationships may find it easier to decide together when sex should be avoided or a condom used.

A link between relationship commitment and the birth control choices of young adults has been reported before as well.

Industry observers note that some surveys pointed to a role for education too. In Arizona, New Jersey and Wisconsin, 55% of cycle trackers had a college degree. Among other birth control users, the figure was 42%.

Recent findings suggest that no consistent link with religion was found. Cycle tracking therefore cannot be explained simply as a religious practice.

Adults aged 25 to 34 were the most likely to track their cycles in three of the four surveys.

It has been revealed that why more people are turning to cycle tracking is still unclear. Some people might just like it better. For others, getting hold of their preferred contraceptive may have become harder.

“Are people choosing these methods because they’re their preferred method, or are they choosing these methods because they’re out of options?” Simmons noted.

“It might be that people are choosing these because they no longer have access to a doctor and they can’t afford the method that they need.”.

According to recent reports, how people track their cycles is another open question. In the surveys, scientifically tested methods could not be told apart from more casual ones.

Industry observers note that many period tracking apps were never designed to prevent pregnancy. Two apps have been cleared for birth control by the US Food and Drug Administration. Only one of them, Natural Cycles, is still on the US market.

The findings have some limits. All birth control habits were self-reported. Other factors that might explain the differences between groups were not accounted for.

The Idaho, Nevada and Utah survey was also carried out online and in English. Some groups in it were small, so the results may not reflect the rest of the country.

Future research could ask cycle trackers directly what led them to choose the method.

Upcoming national data expected in 2027 could reveal whether the growing popularity of cycle tracking reflects a regional trend or a fundamental shift in how Americans approach birth control.

The full study was published in the journal The Lancet Regional Health – Americas.

Latest Update: Scientists find a latest way to study some of the ocean’s most elusive microbes

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new study sheds light on the largely unexplored microbial world beneath the ocean and its potential ecological significance.
  • Industry observers note that most of the microbes living on the deep seafloor have never grown in a lab dish.
  • The sudden change can kill the microbes before anyone gets to study them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new study sheds light on the largely unexplored microbial world beneath the ocean and its potential ecological significance.

Industry observers note that most of the microbes living on the deep seafloor have never grown in a lab dish. On the way to the surface, a sample loses the high pressure and steady cold its microbes are adapted to.

The sudden change can kill the microbes before anyone gets to study them.

A robotic system called DISCUSS keeps both conditions in place, from the seafloor all the way to the lab bench where single microbes are picked out. With it, a team grew a bacterium that barely grows at ordinary air pressure.

Sources indicate that the work was led by Jing-Chun Feng of Guangdong University of Technology in China. Zhengguang Liu, a researcher in the University of Manchester Department of Chemical Engineering, was one of the paper’s corresponding authors.

“Scientists have long struggled to grow many microorganisms found in nature under laboratory conditions, limiting our understanding of how they live and function,” noted Liu.

The deep sea is home to a vast diversity of microbes, many of which have adapted to extreme pressure and near-freezing temperatures.

Some deep-sea microbes even produce enzymes and other molecules.

The molecules that deep-sea microbes create can be useful for medicines, fresh materials, food and energy.

Scientists say that less than one percent of deep-sea microbes can be grown with normal lab techniques.

“Deep-sea microbes are particularly fascinating because they have evolved to survive extreme pressure, cold and unusual chemical conditions,” Liu said.

The testing of this technology was carried out in the South China Sea at a depth of 4,300 feet (1,300 meters) in a cold seep location.

Cold seeps are areas of the seafloor where methane and other compounds emerge at temperatures similar to those of the surrounding water.

At this depth, the water pressure would be 1,900 pounds per square inch (13 megapascals), which is about 130 times the atmospheric pressure at sea level, and water temperature would be 39°F (4°C).

Before carrying out any sampling procedure, sensors detected the levels of methane, carbon dioxide, oxygen, acidity, temperature, and pressure on the seafloor.

After evaluation by the software, only those locations with scores related to methanotrophic microbes were sampled.

The sealed samplers kept more than 98% of the seafloor pressure on the way up.

In the lab, the system built a virtual copy of the seafloor conditions from the sensor readings. Researchers call that kind of copy a digital twin, and the machine used it as the target to hold.

When a sample moved from one chamber to the next, one pump pushed while another pulled at a matched rate. That kept the pressure from jumping during the handoff.

To grow one kind of microbe on its own, a microbiologist spreads cells thinly across a soft gel. Each cell that survives grows into a small dot called a colony.

DISCUSS performs this task inside a sealed, high‑pressure chamber. A robot arm spreads the cells with a needle, and a camera watches through a sapphire window.

It has been revealed that A force sensor in the arm lets it press lightly enough not to tear the gel. In tests, the camera software recognized colonies with 94.6% accuracy.

The needle hit its target within 0.002 inches of the intended spot. Between tasks, the system sterilized the needle using light, keeping the pressure seal intact.

“From an engineering perspective, what excites me most is how intelligent sensing, modeling and automation can help us explore biological systems that were previously difficult to study,” said Liu.

The team recovered 34 microbes and grew each one on its own.

In 11 of them, a gene that scientists use to tell microbes apart differed enough from known reference strains that they may belong to groups not yet described.

According to recent reports, the team took a close look at two of the 34. Both turned out to be strains of known species.

One belongs to Pseudomonas songnenensis, and the other, named HP_SR10, belongs to Bacillus cereus.

To test how much each strain depended on pressure, the researchers grew both for 11 days at five pressures, from ordinary air pressure to a little above the seafloor’s.

The Pseudomonas strain grew about as well at ordinary air pressure as it did at seafloor pressure. HP_SR10 didn’t. It grew best at the same pressure as the seep it came from, and poorly at ordinary air pressure.

The authors wrote that this strain can’t be recovered with conventional methods, which grow microbes at surface pressure.

The system also kept a whole community of microbes alive and working for 180 days.

At its center was a partnership between methane-eating archaea, single-celled microbes distinct from bacteria, and bacteria that use sulfate from seawater.

In a recent development, pumps fed the community methane and nutrients and flushed out waste. That kept sulfide, a byproduct that holds these microbes back at high levels, below 4 millimoles per liter.

Around day 110, both partners became noticeably more common.

The authors wrote that communities like this one typically collapse in closed lab containers with no fresh supply.

Carbon made near the ocean surface can sink to the deep ocean, and scientists still don’t fully understand how deep-sea microbes change it.

Growing a wider range of these microbes under conditions close to home could help scientists study that process.

According to recent reports, only two of the 34 microbes were studied in detail. The study doesn’t describe what the 11 possibly new microbes do, or whether any make useful molecules.

All of the samples also came from a single seep. The authors noted that the design could be adapted for deeper water and for very hot places such as hydrothermal vents.

Next, the team prepares to run many plates at once under different conditions and to track dissolved chemicals more closely as they change.

The researchers also plan to automate growing microbes in liquid instead of on gel.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Sensors.

In a 1996 study, researchers reviewed 22,793 poinsettia cases reported to U.S. poison centers and found no deaths, but the plant can still upset pets

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (745 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Poison Control says the deadly reputation rests on a child's death over 100 years ago.
  • Every holiday season, poinsettias go up on tables and windowsills, and so does an old warning: keep them away from children, because they are deadly.
  • Researchers led by the Pittsburgh Poison Center checked that idea against hard numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Poison Control says the deadly reputation rests on a child's death over 100 years ago. Tests of about 500 to 600 leaves found no poisonous dose.

Every holiday season, poinsettias go up on tables and windowsills, and so does an old warning: keep them away from children, because they are deadly.

Researchers led by the Pittsburgh Poison Center checked that idea against hard numbers. In a study published in 1996 in the American Journal of Emergency Medicine, they analyzed 849,575 plant exposures reported to the American Association of Poison Control Centers (HRSA).

Poinsettias accounted for 22,793 of those cases. There were no deaths among them.

The researchers wrote that the poinsettia “is a much-maligned plant which is thought by the public and some health professionals to be extremely toxic.”.

Their data told a different story. Almost all of the poinsettia exposures, 98.9%, were accidental, and 93.3% involved children.

Sources indicate that most of the people involved, 96.1%, were not treated in a health care facility. And 92.4% did not develop any toxicity related to the poinsettia at all.

“Most patients do not require any type of therapy and can be treated without referral to a health care facility,” the authors concluded.

The study is 30 years old, but the current advice from Poison Control, run by the National Capital Poison Center, claims the same thing.

In a recent development, “The poinsettia plant is often considered deadly. That’s wrong,” its guidance states. “Poinsettia can be irritating but it is not fatal if eaten.”.

Poison Control says some stories “just won’t go away.” “Over a hundred years ago, a child was found next to a wild poinsettia plant. He died and people blamed the plant. This hasn’t happened since,” it says.

Sources indicate that researchers have even tried to find a poisonous dose. They “just couldn’t, even after reaching experimental doses of about 1.25 pounds (500-600 leaves),” according to Poison Control.

Sources indicate that that does not mean the plant is a snack. If children or pets eat it, Poison Control says, they can develop mouth irritation and stomach upset, such as nausea, vomiting or diarrhea.

The sap can cause a skin rash, and Poison Control notes reports of gardeners who work with the plant frequently developing one.

Poison Control describes one real case. On Christmas Day, a 10-month-old put a small piece of a poinsettia leaf in his mouth, and his mother called a poison center.

The specialist told her no problems were expected and advised her to wipe the child’s mouth and give him something to drink.

The plant can also be a choking hazard, so Poison Control recommends placing poinsettias, and other houseplants, where children and pets cannot reach them.

The ASPCA lists the poinsettia as toxic to dogs, cats and horses, and it names the plant’s irritant sap as the toxic principle.

Under clinical signs, the ASPCA describes the plant as “irritating to the mouth and stomach, sometimes causing vomiting, but generally over-rated in toxicity.”.

Sources indicate that poinsettias are only one of the season’s concerns for pet owners. Earth.com has looked at how to keep cats safe at Christmas, from toxic trees to dangling decorations, and at festive plants that may be less safe than they look.

The poinsettia is the most popular flowering plant sold in the United States, with more than 70 million sold each year, according to a Clemson Cooperative Extension factsheet last revised in 2015.

Industry observers note that it is named after Joel R. Poinsett, the first U.S. ambassador to Mexico. He brought the plant to the Bartram Botanical Garden in Philadelphia in 1828, and a Philadelphia nurseryman, Robert Buist, named it after him, the factsheet claims.

It has been revealed that the wild plants in Mexico grew 12 to 15 feet tall. The red parts that people think of as flowers are actually bracts, a kind of modified leaf. The true flowers are the small yellow clusters in the center.

If someone does swallow part of a poinsettia, Poison Control’s advice is to call a poison center at 1-800-222-1222, which is free, confidential and available 24 hours a day.

The information was obtained from the study Poinsettia exposures have good outcomes…just as we thought (American Journal of Emergency Medicine, 1996), Poison Control’s page Are poinsettias poisonous?, the ASPCA’s poinsettia entry, and Clemson Cooperative Extension’s poinsettia factsheet.

Recent findings suggest that these days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” says the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.

Some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

Industry observers note that not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih states. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.

In a recent development, the hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih notes—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a latest drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.

Interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen says.

Another outstanding question, Yih says, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.

Recent findings suggest that women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.

Sources indicate that rowen currently has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for latest treatments is there, Rowen says. “Women deserve better than placebo.”.

Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

💡 Key Takeaways
  • FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday.
  • President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.
  • Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.

Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.

Much of the hearing focused on Carr and his threats to use the FCC to punish broadcasters he disagrees with.

Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., said that he expects Carr will not last long in his position once Democrats take control of Congress in the newly introduced year.

“Mr. Carr, if you're listening now, know you're going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions … so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place,” Luján noted.

The nomination of Thumann Severs, who currently serves as senior counsel to Carr, has led to consternation among Democrats due to continued vacancies at the FCC. The five-member commission is intended to have three members of the president’s party, including the chair, and two in the minority.

Currently Carr serves alongside fellow Republican Olivia Trusty and Democrat Anna M. Gomez, whose term expired earlier this year. Gomez may continue to serve through next year under the law if a replacement is not nominated and confirmed.

Democrats are concerned that if Thumann Severs were to be confirmed, the commission’s three Republican members could constitute a quorum on their own, allowing Trump to fire Gomez.

According to recent reports, sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., noted Senate precedent is to move pairs of one Democratic and one Republican nominee for the FCC and that he “strongly” believed the Thumann Severs nomination should have been paired with a renomination of Gomez in order to continue having “both parties at the table.”.

“A bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation [and] I think also, more fundamentally, to protect a free and diverse press [that] serves everyone,” Hickenlooper said.

In addition to urging Trump to renominate Gomez, Democrats underlined the need for a second Democratic member of the commission.

Hickenlooper highlighted Thumann Severs’ close work with Carr, who Democrats and some Republicans have been critical of for comments about using the FCC’s public interest standard against television stations airing programming Carr disagrees with.

Thumann Severs’ work at the FCC presently focuses on the Wireline, Public Safety and Homeland Security, and Consumer and Governmental Affairs bureaus, rather than the Media Bureau.

Committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has also been critical of Carr’s comments. On Tuesday, he listed the FCC’s request for ABC-owned stations to submit early license renewals alongside earlier incidents in which he said Democrats encouraged the weaponization of the FCC against conservative voices.

According to recent reports, “The First Amendment places notable limits on the government’s ability to regulate speech,” Cruz remarked. “The FCC possesses significant regulatory authority over communications, so there is always a risk that it could weaponize its authority against Americans with whom it disagrees.”.

Thumann Severs committed to Cruz that she would base licensing decisions on “the law and the record” and not use the FCC’s authority to “pressure or punish” broadcasters for protected speech.

In a recent development, however, when Sen. Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., questioned Thumann Severs on whether the FCC could punish broadcasters the president disagreed with, Thumann Severs repeated one of Carr’s arguments in discussing the FCC’s role.

In a recent development, “Broadcasters are subject to public interest obligations as part of the public trustee model in exchange for the licenses that they hold,” she said. “As part of those public interest obligations, they are subject to many different rules and requirements, and the FCC is charged with enforcing and investigating the public interest standard against broadcasters.”.

Under repeated questions from Markey about Carr’s previous remarks, Thumann Severs said she would base her decisions “in the facts and the law and the record.”.

Industry observers note that luján also asked Thumann Severs to name concerns where she had disagreed with Carr or Trump. While she stated her decisions would be her own, she declined to name any examples of disagreement.

In addition to questions about Carr, Democrats asked the nominee about the FCC’s E-Rate program, which provides low-cost connectivity for schools and libraries, and the Universal Service Fund, which funds the E-Rate program and other programs.

Thumann Severs stated that she believes the E-Rate program has been successful and that the FCC has a statutory obligation to provide some kind of discounted service to schools and libraries. But she was less forthcoming on whether the FCC could shut down the program as it currently exists without congressional approval or whether the program should be restricted only to rural areas.

Late last month, Democratic members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, led by Communications and Technology Subcommittee ranking member Doris Matsui, D-Calif., sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Cruz urging Gomez’s renomination with any move to confirm a Republican nominee.

In a recent development, “Commissioner Gomez has shown the experience and judgment to continue that work,” the members wrote. “We therefore ask that the Senate pair any new Republican nominee with her renomination to a full term, consistent with the bipartisan design Congress built into this agency.”.

On Monday, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights also sent a letter to committee leadership urging a delay on the hearing and any vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination until Gomez can be renominated.

“Independent agencies should not be extensions of presidential will: their leaders should exercise independent judgement based on their expertise and statutory mandates,” the group wrote.

Cruz did not indicate Tuesday when the committee might vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination, and no markup has yet been announced by the committee of hers' and those of three others for two posts at NASA and one at the Transportation Department who also testified.

An mRNA shot made hearts pump about 10% more blood after a heart attack, with the effect lasting 12 weeks

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An experimental mRNA treatment helped mouse heart cells divide after a heart attack, improving pumping function, but human trials are still needed.
  • An experimental treatment pushed adult heart muscle cells in mice to divide again after a heart attack, something those cells normally cannot do.
  • Researchers at the University of Cambridge delivered a modified messenger RNA that briefly switches on two proteins inside heart cells, Myc and Cyclin T1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An experimental mRNA treatment helped mouse heart cells divide after a heart attack, improving pumping function, but human trials are still needed.

An experimental treatment pushed adult heart muscle cells in mice to divide again after a heart attack, something those cells normally cannot do.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge delivered a modified messenger RNA that briefly switches on two proteins inside heart cells, Myc and Cyclin T1.

Treated mice pumped around 10 percent more blood with each heartbeat than mice given a mock treatment, the university reported.

In a recent development, the gain held when the animals were reassessed at 12 weeks. The work was done in mice, and the treatment has not been tested in people.

Sources indicate that an adult human heart can lose up to one billion heart muscle cells in a heart attack. Those cells are never replaced, which weakens the pump and leaves scar tissue behind.

It has been revealed that an estimated 920,000 people in the U.K. are living with heart failure, and a transplant is the only cure, according to the British Heart Foundation (BHF).

“Getting the human heart to repair itself is the holy grail for cardiologists,” stated Professor Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the BHF.

Myc is better known as a cancer gene. Switching it on makes liver cells multiply within days, yet in the heart it does almost nothing.

A 2020 mouse study explained why. Myc protein binds DNA in heart muscle cells but cannot turn genes on, because the heart is short of a partner protein, Cyclin T1.

In a recent development, “When the Ccnt1 and Myc genes were expressed together, the heart switched into a regenerative state,” noted Dr. Megan Bywater, a senior research officer at QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute and first author of that work.

Industry observers note that the new experiment turns that finding into something closer to a therapy. Instead of altering genes, it uses mRNA, the kind of instruction a cell reads and then breaks down.

The team injected 100 micrograms of modified mRNA straight into the heart muscle during surgery. Injections guided by ultrasound did not work efficiently.

Myc and Cyclin T1 protein demonstrated up in heart tissue one hour and four hours after the injection, and had gone by 24 hours.

A fluorescent version of the molecule, used to track where it travelled, was still visible around damaged heart cells 24 hours after the injection.

The university states the brief, localized signal is not expected to cause any permanent modification, which is meant to limit the risk of overgrowth.

Ultrasound scans tracked each animal on days three, six and 28 after treatment.

Recent findings suggest that ejection fraction, the share of blood the left ventricle pushes out with each beat, dropped by 26 percent in treated mice by day 28. In untreated animals it fell by 37 percent.

At 12 weeks the decline was 7.1 percent in the treated group, against 16.1 percent in controls.

Markers of cell division rose in the treated hearts, and the number of heart muscle cells had climbed by day five.

Tagging cells and their descendants showed 41.5 percent of labeled heart muscle cells sitting in adjacent pairs after treatment, compared with 5.5 percent in control hearts.

A genetically engineered version of the same approach did even better, holding the day-28 decline to 9 percent against 23 percent in controls.

Scar tissue told a different story. By day 28 the scar was no smaller in treated mice, although the volume of working muscle in the left ventricle had grown.

Waiting did not ruin the effect. In the transgenic model, switching the two proteins on seven to eight days later held the ejection fraction drop to 14 percent by day 36, against 30 percent in untreated animals.

No tumors were found in the treated animals at either checkpoint, and laboratory tests found no added capacity to transform cells.

Switching Myc on across the whole heart, by contrast, killed seven of eight mice in the transgenic version of the experiment, which is why the team confined the signal to the injured area.

Among the animals that received the mRNA, survival across 12 weeks did not differ significantly from controls.

Human heart muscle cells grown from stem cells in a dish also revealed more signs of division after treatment.

The Cambridge group is now refining the treatment with BHF funding.

Larger animal studies, and then human trials, are needed to establish safety and effectiveness before the approach could help a human heart heal after a heart attack.

“These are really exciting results,” stated Dr. Catherine Wilson, an associate professor of pharmacology at the University of Cambridge and co-senior author of the study.

“We’re not just treating the symptoms of heart failure – this approach could help the heart to repair itself,” Wilson added.

“That makes it exciting when studies like this are able to reignite regeneration in heart muscle cells,” Williams said.

The study was published in the journal Nature Cardiovascular Research.

Latest Update: Extreme weather in India and China shared a hidden atmospheric connection
