💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new analysis reveals how atmospheric circulation connected extreme heat in India with a rapid shift from flooding to humid heat in southern China.
  • India baked under a stubborn heat dome while southern China lurched from flooding into dangerous, humid heat.
  • A latest analysis links the May 2026 extremes to the same sprawling high-pressure system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new analysis reveals how atmospheric circulation connected extreme heat in India with a rapid shift from flooding to humid heat in southern China.

India baked under a stubborn heat dome while southern China lurched from flooding into dangerous, humid heat.

A latest analysis links the May 2026 extremes to the same sprawling high-pressure system.

Meng Gao from Hong Kong Baptist University led the analysis, with collaborators from the Chinese Academy of Meteorological Sciences and Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology.

For much of early May, temperatures across the Indian region studied had been below normal.

Starting on May 17, that changed sharply, with temperatures staying over 1°C above the recent May average.

The researchers combined weather observations, atmospheric reanalysis, and climate simulations to trace the change.

Their maps demonstrated daily average temperatures exceeding 40°C in some locations.

According to recent reports, may 20 stood out. Across the region studied, it was the hottest May 20 in the record stretching back to 1979.

It has been revealed that humidity added to the strain. The wet-bulb temperature, which reflects the combined effects of heat and moisture, ranked third-highest for that date.

For people working outside, particularly in northern India, the combination made an already difficult season more dangerous.

Sources indicate that the developing El Niño offered part of the explanation. By May, the central and eastern equatorial Pacific had entered El Niño conditions.

Atmospheric circulation shifted far beyond its shores.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers linked this developing El Niño to a stronger western Pacific subtropical high. This broad area of high pressure also stretched farther west than usual.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, a persistent wave pattern in the upper atmosphere strengthened another high-pressure system over the Iranian Plateau. That system moved eastward.

Over India, the two highs joined, creating a stable “heat dome.” Air sank beneath it, warming as it descended and helping keep skies clear.

Industry observers note that with more sunshine reaching the ground, temperatures continued rising. Warm waters in the northern Indian Ocean also helped strengthen the Pacific high, further supporting the persistent heat.

In southern China, the same Pacific high helped produce a different sequence of hazards.

Guangdong had endured repeated downpours since early May.

Particularly heavy rain between May 19 and 23 brought widespread flooding, followed almost immediately by humid heat from May 24–29.

According to recent reports, the abrupt switch followed the high-pressure system’s movement northwestward. Rain eased, sunshine increased, and descending air warmed the region.

The atmosphere, however, remained laden with moisture after the downpours. The result was a “rainfall-to-deadly humid heat” sequence, with little time between the two emergencies.

The paper reports dozens of heatstroke ambulance calls in Shenzhen and thousands of livestock deaths in Maoming.

Such dangerous combinations of heat and humidity arrived one to two months earlier than usual.

In a recent development, air temperatures alone did not explain what happened in Guangdong. Readings were near the top of the historical range, but comparable heat had occurred before.

In a recent development, the difference was the moisture accompanying them. Relative humidity during the dangerous hours averaged about 60%, compared with roughly 50% during similarly hot hours in earlier years.

Recent findings suggest that humid air makes it harder for sweat to evaporate, limiting the body’s ability to shed heat. That means familiar thermometer readings can conceal much greater physical strain.

Industry observers note that for several hours, conditions exceeded a modeled threshold for safe, sustained activity among healthy adults aged 65 or older. That applied even to sitting quietly or standing with minimal movement.

Industry observers note that that threshold describes a particular group under specified conditions. Heat tolerance varies with age, activity, and exposure to sunlight.

The timing was exceptional too: these conditions appeared earlier than in any year of the available 2011–2025 comparison record.

The team also asked how human influence had changed the likelihood of India’s heat.

Using 11 climate models, the researchers compared simulations including human influences with a preindustrial climate.

Their central estimate suggested human influences had made a similarly intense Indian heatwave roughly 27 times more likely.

The estimated range was wide: about 16 to 52 times, at a 90% confidence level. The authors caution that differences between models and limitations in correcting their biases affect the result.

In a recent development, the authors describe the finding as evidence of a likely human contribution, with the precise scale still uncertain. The estimate applies to the Indian event, not to the entire sequence across both countries.

A common atmospheric influence helps explain why distant places suffered heat at nearly the same time. Whether those heatwaves also reinforced each other remains unresolved.

It has been revealed that for southern China, the order of events matters. Flooding can damage electricity supplies and other infrastructure, leaving residents without reliable cooling when the heat follows.

Warnings therefore need to account for what happened in the preceding days.

A heat forecast issued during flood recovery may reach people whose homes, workplaces, and access to electricity are already disrupted.

The researchers call for stronger infrastructure and better preparation in vulnerable regions.

In places facing rapid weather reversals, flood response and heat preparation may need to happen at the same time.

The study is published in the journal Advances in Atmospheric Sciences.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In his journal entry for that day, Carter recorded his reply to Lord Carnarvon as 'Yes, it is wonderful.' The famous line comes from his 1923 book.
  • On November 26, 1922, in Egypt’s Valley of the Kings, Howard Carter held a candle up to a small hole in a sealed doorway and looked into the tomb of Tutankhamun for the first time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In his journal entry for that day, Carter recorded his reply to Lord Carnarvon as 'Yes, it is wonderful.' The famous line comes from his 1923 book.

On November 26, 1922, in Egypt’s Valley of the Kings, Howard Carter held a candle up to a small hole in a sealed doorway and looked into the tomb of Tutankhamun for the first time.

Sources indicate that what he said next is one of the most quoted lines in archaeology. In his published account, Carter, asked whether he could see anything, answered, “Yes, wonderful things.”.

But in the journal he kept during the excavation, Carter wrote down a different reply.

Recent findings suggest that carter’s handwritten journal for the first season of work on the tomb is held by the Griffith Institute at the University of Oxford, which has published a transcript online. Its entry for November 26, 1922, describes the moment step by step.

That afternoon, after clearing 9 meters (about 30 feet) of a descending passage, the team reached a second sealed doorway.

Carter made “a tiny breach in the top left hand corner to see what was beyond.” Candles were brought, he wrote, as a test for foul gases.

Carter’s patron, Lord Carnarvon, his daughter Lady Evelyn Herbert and Carter’s colleague Arthur Callender waited “in anxious expectation,” Carter wrote. “It was sometime before one could see, the hot air escaping caused the candle to flicker,” he added.

Then the room appeared, “with its strange and wonderful medley of extraordinary and beautiful objects heaped upon one another.”.

According to recent reports, “There was naturally short suspense for those present who could not see, when Lord Carnarvon mentioned to me ‘Can you see anything’. I replied to him Yes, it is wonderful,” the entry reads.

Recent findings suggest that the more famous version appeared in 1923 in the first volume of “The Tomb of Tut.Ankh.Amen,” credited to Carter and A. C. Mace, an associate curator at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

In the book, Carter describes seeing “strange animals, statues, and gold” and “everywhere the glint of gold.”.

He writes that he was “struck dumb with amazement,” and that when Carnarvon asked, “Can you see anything?” it was all he could do “to get out the words, ‘Yes, wonderful things.'”.

The journal does not settle exactly what Carter noted out loud in that passageway. But it shows that the line most people know comes from the book, not from the words Carter wrote in his journal.

Sources indicate that the journal entry goes on to list what the light revealed. Carter wrote of “two strange ebony-black effigies of a King, gold sandalled, bearing staff and mace,” gilded couches, painted caskets, alabaster vases, “a golden inlaid throne” and “a confusion of overturned parts of chariots glinting with gold.”.

His first impression, he wrote, was of “the property-room of an opera-house of a vanished civilization.”.

Industry observers note that the team was not even sure it had found a royal burial. Even that afternoon, Carter wrote, the passage had seemed to support “our first conjecture that we had found a cache.”.

Then they saw a sealed doorway between two guardian statues and the name of Tutankhamun on most of the objects.

Recent findings suggest that “Was it a tomb or merely a cache?” Carter asked in the journal. With the evidence in front of them, he concluded, “there was little doubt that there behind was the grave of that Pharaoh.”.

The next day, Callender set up electric lights, and the group made a careful inspection of the room, which came to be called the Antechamber.

Industry observers note that the look inside came 22 days after the first sign of the tomb. According to the Griffith Institute, Carter’s journal covers the discovery of the tomb’s stairway on November 4, 1922, and the uncovering of the first sealed doorway on November 5.

On November 4, Carter wrote, “At about 10am I discovered beneath almost the first hut attacked the first traces of the entrance of the tomb.” By sunset the next day, the workers had cleared down to the 12th step and exposed the top of a plastered, sealed doorway.

It has been revealed that carter then sent a cable to Carnarvon, who was in England. “At last have made wonderful discovery in Valley a magnificent tomb with seals intact recovered same for your arrival congratulations,” it read, as copied into the journal.

More than a century later, the tomb still needs protecting. Earth.com has reported on cracks from water damage that threaten King Tut’s painted tomb and on another long-lost royal tomb that has emerged in Egypt.

Sources indicate that the information was obtained from Howard Carter’s journal for the 1922-23 excavation season, as transcribed by the Griffith Institute, University of Oxford, and from the first volume of The Tomb of Tut.Ankh.Amen by Howard Carter and A. C. Mace (1923).

#158672. Cougars battle deep snow and freezing weather every winter, but nature is not what kills most of them

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1180 w)

Cougars battle deep snow and freezing weather every winter, but nature is not what kills most of them

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1180 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, people, not weather, caused most deaths among tracked cougars.
  • You might expect deep snow and bitter cold to be the biggest threat to a wild animal in winter.
  • Recent findings suggest that of 80 cougars fitted with tracking collars, 37 died, and people caused 29 of those deaths.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, people, not weather, caused most deaths among tracked cougars. The hunting season, roads, and human houses each play a role.

You might expect deep snow and bitter cold to be the biggest threat to a wild animal in winter. Yet when researchers tracked cougars across five winters in the foothills of Alberta’s Rocky Mountains, they found the weather was not what killed them. People were.

Recent findings suggest that of 80 cougars fitted with tracking collars, 37 died, and people caused 29 of those deaths. Nearly all of them came between November and March, and Alberta’s cougar hunting season falls inside those months.

Industry observers note that where a cougar spent its time mattered too. Cats that stayed close to houses and unpaved roads died at higher rates than cats that kept away from them.

Carter Littlefair and Andrew Derocher of the University of Alberta’s Department of Biological Sciences led the study. Their co-authors, Paul Frame and Mark Edwards, work at Alberta Environment and Protected Areas, the province’s environment ministry.

In a recent development, between 2016 and 2021, the team used hounds to tree cougars in the country south of Whitecourt and north of Sundre. They then darted each cat and fitted a GPS collar. The collars reported a location every seven hours.

Recent findings suggest that the 80 cats were followed for a little over a year each, on average. When a collar signaled a death, crew reached the site within three days to work out what had happened.

Hunters killed 16 of the 37 that died. Another eight died in traps set for other animals, and two were hit by vehicles. Three more were killed as problem animals or by landowners with permission.

Wolves killed three adult females, two of them with kittens still depending on them. Seven deaths in all were natural, and one could not be explained. The cats share this country with wolves, black bears, and grizzlies, and their main prey is white-tailed deer.

In an average year, a collared cougar had a 60 percent chance of living through the next 12 months. That figure hides a split between the seasons.

It has been revealed that from April through October, 96 percent of the cats survived. From November through March, only 62 percent did.

In a recent development, cougar hunting in the study area opens on December 1 and closes at the end of February, or earlier once an area’s quota is filled. Hunters there use hounds to follow a track and tree the cat. Of the 37 cougars that died, 33 died in the cold months.

Since 2019, the province has set each area’s hunting quota at roughly 14 to 16 percent of the cougars it estimates live there.

In an interview with Earth.com, Littlefair stated that lowering harvest limits would have the greatest direct effect on survival, since hunting caused the majority of the deaths the team documented.

Alberta’s system lets each management area’s limits be adjusted every year, separately for males and females, and the findings can help inform how they are set, Littlefair remarked.

Sources indicate that the team then asked which parts of the landscape went with dying. Rugged terrain and forest edges, which the team expected to make a cat easier to spot or reach, made no difference to survival.

It has been revealed that what mattered was access. A cougar within about 490 feet (150 meters) of a house faced a much higher risk of death than one farther away. So did a cougar within about 165 feet (50 meters) of an unpaved road.

The authors suggested a reason: a hound hunt begins with a track rather than a sighting, and hunters find those tracks along roads and cutlines before the chase starts.

“Mortality risk increased with proximity to residences and secondary roads, indicating that cougars occupying accessible areas were more vulnerable to harvest,” they wrote.

Cats that crossed cutlines, pipelines, power lines, and seismic lines more often as they traveled were also more likely to die. Logging and oil and gas work have left this part of Alberta with a dense network of unpaved roads.

Littlefair said that reducing the density of roads and other human-made disturbances across the landscape could also help lower that risk.

Recent findings suggest that familiar ground did not seem to protect them either. Of 15 cougars whose previous year’s range could be mapped, 12 died inside it.

It has been revealed that alberta’s rules are built to steer hunters toward males. Quotas allow more males than females, and a female with kittens is off limits. Hunters using hounds also tend to select large males.

So the team expected males to die more frequently, as they do in hunted populations elsewhere. They didn’t find that and Littlefair told Earth.com it was one of the more surprising results.

Industry observers note that other studies with similarly female-heavy samples have still found hunters taking more males. In this study, however, hunters killed nine females and seven males, and the team could not detect any difference in survival between the sexes.

Recent findings suggest that hunting did make up a bigger share of male deaths, with 64 percent in comparison to 35 percent for females. But with only 24 males in the study, that difference could have come up by chance.

Mothers were at no extra risk the team could detect: it found 18 litters, and females with kittens survived at the same rate as females without them.

Hunting’s 43 percent share of the deaths is smaller than the 62 to 75 percent reported in some other hunted cougar populations. Provincial records also show human-caused cougar deaths have fallen since a peak in 2015.

“One important distinction is that high mortality does not necessarily indicate an unsustainable population,” Littlefair said.

Judging that would require counts that the study did not make, of the cougars there, their kittens, and the young that reach adulthood.

The study did not measure how many hunters were out or how hard they hunted, so it can’t separate a road from the people driving on it.

The authors treat a cat’s use of roads and houses as a stand-in for its chances of meeting a hunter, not as a danger in itself.

A second gap is the number of males. With 56 females and 24 males collared, the study can say less about males.

“It would certainly be interesting to repeat the study with a more balanced sample of males and females to see whether this pattern persists,” Littlefair mentioned.

For now, the finding covers one stretch of Alberta, where a cougar’s odds of surviving the winter depend on how close it lives to a house or an unpaved road.

Littlefair and his team believe that managers should weigh that pattern of access when they judge how much hunting a population can absorb, and where it falls.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS One.

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It was an unprecedented year for El Niño, the weather-changing ocean pattern defined by warmer-than-normal surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. By October 18, the ocean area that researchers use to monitor El Niño’s severity climbed to an average temperature of over 30° Celsius (86° Fahrenheit) for the first time in history. From there, it kept on rising.

In September, the region’s daily average sea surface temperature reached the most extreme level ever recorded: more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average (dashed line). The World Meteorological Organization predicts that sea surface temperatures may peak at 3.7 degrees above that average by January. The two previous strongest El Niños on record emerged in 1997 and 2015.

According to recent reports, all that hot water has fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record. By mid-October, 331 units of cyclone energy had accumulated, beating out 2018’s record of 318 units. It has also unleashed heat into the atmosphere, affecting distant circulation patterns and leading to an extraordinarily quiet Atlantic hurricane season.

Industry observers note that 2026’s El Niño will be felt well beyond the Newly introduced Year. Precipitation and drought impacts are expected across the world through spring 2027. And the global heating effect could compound with human-caused climate warming to make 2027 the hottest year ever recorded.

The heat that El Niño unleashes into the atmosphere shifts storm tracks and weather patterns globally. Here are some of the most significant observed and anticipated effects.

#158670. Komodo dragons have a thin layer of iron on their teeth that keeps them razor-sharp for tearing apart prey

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (791 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Komodo dragons have a thin layer of iron on their teeth that keeps them razor-sharp for tearing apart prey

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers discovered that Komodo dragons coat the serrated edges of their teeth in iron, staining them orange and keeping them razor-sharp for ripping apart prey.
  • Recent findings suggest that look closely at a Komodo dragon’s teeth, and you will notice an orange tint along the cutting edges.
  • Recent findings suggest that the color actually comes from iron.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers discovered that Komodo dragons coat the serrated edges of their teeth in iron, staining them orange and keeping them razor-sharp for ripping apart prey.

Recent findings suggest that look closely at a Komodo dragon’s teeth, and you will notice an orange tint along the cutting edges. It is not a stain from feeding. Even teeth that have not yet pushed through the gums are just as orange.

Recent findings suggest that the color actually comes from iron. In a 2024 study, researchers found a thin, iron-rich coating along the tips and serrated edges, concluding that it helps keep the teeth sharp.

Scientists had never seen anything like it in a meat-eating reptile before.

“Komodo dragons have curved, serrated teeth to rip and tear their prey just like those of meat-eating dinosaurs,” said Aaron LeBlanc of King’s College London, the study’s lead author.

In a recent development, leBlanc’s team looked for the same coating on fossil dinosaur teeth and saw no evidence of it. But fossilization may be the reason.

Industry observers note that komodo dragons are the largest predatory lizards alive, and scientists have studied their teeth before. One detail had still been overlooked.

LeBlanc’s team examined teeth from skeletons and from specimens preserved in fluid. Every unworn tooth tip and serration was orange.

Serrations are the small points along a cutting edge, like the ones on a steak knife.

In a recent development, the rest of each tooth looked white. The enamel there is transparent, so the white comes from the layer underneath, called dentin.

Recent findings suggest that the enamel on a Komodo dragon’s serrations and tooth tips is about 0.0008 inches (20 micrometers) thick. That’s roughly one-fifth the thickness of a sheet of printer paper.

Sources indicate that the team found iron in the outermost layer of that enamel with every method it used. At its thickest, the iron-rich layer makes up about a tenth of the enamel’s thickness.

Recent findings suggest that one of those methods was X-ray mapping at a type of particle accelerator called a synchrotron. Those maps showed the iron concentrated along the serrations.

Sources indicate that with another method, the team found more oxygen where the iron was concentrated. The authors took that as a sign the coating is an iron oxide. Rust is made of iron oxides too.

How hard is the coating? On a Komodo dragon tooth, LeBlanc’s team found that difficult to test reliably, because the coating is so thin.

So the team turned to a tooth shed by an American alligator at a British zoo. That tooth had iron-rich enamel thick enough to test.

It has been revealed that to test it, the team pressed a fine tip into the enamel of that one tooth 74 times. The iron-rich enamel was slightly harder than the enamel beneath it, by about 9%.

Like the team’s electron microscope and X-ray experiments, the hardness tests were each run once, on individual teeth.

Recent findings suggest that iron may make the outer enamel along a cutting edge more resistant to wear. For the Komodo dragon, that’s less certain. Its iron-rich layer is much thinner than the alligator’s.

Still, worn Komodo dragon teeth hint that the coating protects the serrations. Enamel can flake off most of a worn tooth and expose the dentin. On the serrations, the enamel appears to wear down gradually instead.

Komodo dragons replace their teeth swiftly. So the thin coating must be enough to keep each tooth sharp until a upcoming one takes its place, the authors wrote.

Meat-eating dinosaurs had serrated teeth with thin enamel, just as Komodo dragons do.

Recent findings suggest that the team also tested teeth shed by crocodiles and their relatives living in zoos. All four species, the American alligator among them, had an iron-rich outer layer of enamel.

So the team looked for iron in fossil teeth from tyrannosaurs and from the family that includes Velociraptor. Every technique gave the same result. The team saw no consistent sign of extra iron in the enamel on the serrations.

Sources indicate that leBlanc’s team gave two possible explanations. Either fossilization masks the iron, or these dinosaurs didn’t normally concentrate it along their serrations. For now, the fossils can’t show which explanation is right.

“With further analysis of the Komodo teeth we may be able to find other markers in the iron coating that aren’t changed during fossilization,” LeBlanc noted.

“With markers like that we would know with certainty whether dinosaurs also had iron-coated teeth and have a greater understanding of these ferocious predators.”.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution.

In 1958, the Hope Diamond went to the Smithsonian by mail for $2.44 in postage, and the museum says a jeweler likely embellished its curse to sell it

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A jeweler's employee paid $145.29 to mail the 45.52-carat blue gem from New York, nearly all of it to insure it for $1 million.
  • Sources indicate that on November 8, 1958, an employee of Harry Winston’s jewelry store in Newly introduced York City mailed an ordinary-looking package.
  • The employee paid $145.29 to send it to the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., according to the Smithsonian’s National Postal Museum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A jeweler's employee paid $145.29 to mail the 45.52-carat blue gem from New York, nearly all of it to insure it for $1 million.

Sources indicate that on November 8, 1958, an employee of Harry Winston’s jewelry store in Newly introduced York City mailed an ordinary-looking package. Inside was the Hope Diamond.

The employee paid $145.29 to send it to the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., according to the Smithsonian’s National Postal Museum. Only $2.44 of that was postage. The rest paid for $1 million in insurance.

It has been revealed that the 45.52-carat blue diamond traveled by registered mail in a plain brown wrapper. It is still on display at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, and the museum has a short answer for anyone who asks whether it carries a curse.

According to recent reports, “Is the Hope Diamond cursed? Of course not!” the museum says on its history of the gem.

In Washington, local letter carrier James G. Todd picked up the package at the city post office, a building that now houses the National Postal Museum.

Leonard Carmichael, the Secretary of the Smithsonian, brought Todd into the Gem Hall, where reporters and cameras watched him pull the package from his mail satchel and hand it over, the Postal Museum recounts.

Industry observers note that the Natural History Museum dates the arrival to November 10, 1958. Harry Winston’s wife presented the diamond to Carmichael and to George S. Switzer, the museum’s curator of mineralogy. It “almost immediately became its premier attraction,” according to the museum.

Industry observers note that the diamond’s history is far older. The Smithsonian traces it to a blue diamond of about 115 carats known as Tavernier’s Diamond, after the French merchant Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, which King Louis XIV had recut.

It must have come from India, the museum states, since India was the only commercial source of diamonds in Tavernier’s time.

Industry observers note that the curse is much younger. “The story of a curse is a recent part of the diamond’s history, apparently having its origins in the early 20th century,” the museum indicates.

One early account ran in the Washington Post in January 1908. According to the Smithsonian, it offered “a selective history” of the gem, listing the bad luck of earlier owners. Later versions of the curse followed the same pattern.

A November 1909 newspaper report that a former owner, the Turkish diamond merchant Selim Habib, had drowned with the gem when a steamer sank at Singapore added to the legend.

The museum calls that report “wildly inaccurate.” Neither Habib nor the diamond was on the ship, and he had already sold the stone in June 1909.

The Smithsonian says some of the people who spread the curse stories may have done so for their own gain.

The French jewelry house Cartier bought the Hope Diamond in 1910, and Pierre Cartier set out to sell it. Intriguing histories helped sell gems in those years.

“Cartier thus began to fabricate a fanciful story around the Hope Diamond that included a curse, which he would pitch to potential buyers,” the museum writes.

Recent findings suggest that he pitched it to Ned and Evalyn Walsh McLean, and the sale took two years. In the Smithsonian’s words, Cartier “likely embellished the stories as a sales tactic.”.

Sources indicate that the tale did not scare Evalyn McLean off. She told Cartier she believed objects that brought bad luck to others would bring good luck to her.

After he had the stone reset and left it with the couple for a weekend, she agreed to buy it in 1912 for $180,000 plus the return of a pendant she no longer wanted.

May Yohé, who was once married to Lord Francis Hope, an earlier owner, helped make the curse a popular modern legend.

In a book and a film released in 1921, she blamed the diamond for her failed marriage and the loss of the Hope family fortune, according to the Smithsonian.

It has been revealed that after Evalyn McLean died in 1947, Harry Winston bought her jewelry, including the Hope Diamond, in 1949. He demonstrated it across the United States in a traveling exhibition called the Court of Jewels before giving it to the Smithsonian.

At the donation ceremony, Winston’s wife scoffed at the idea of a curse and noted that her family had held the gem without any ill effects.

It has been revealed that todd, the letter carrier, had a harder time. Within a year of the delivery, he was hurt in two separate car accidents, his wife died of a heart attack, his dog strangled on its leash and his home in Seat Pleasant, Maryland, was partly destroyed by fire, according to the Postal Museum.

Recent findings suggest that he still did not blame the diamond. “I don’t believe any of that stuff,” he told a reporter.

“If the hex is supposed to affect the owners, then the public should be having the bad luck,” he added.

The diamond stayed at the Natural History Museum, and the brown paper wrapper it came in is now part of the National Postal Museum’s collection.

Sources indicate that the Hope’s deep blue color has its own science story. Earth.com has reported that some blue diamonds formed hundreds of miles below Earth’s surface.

The Smithsonian has hidden history of its own, including a secret chamber from 1847 found beneath the Smithsonian Castle.

The information was obtained from the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History’s History of the Hope Diamond and the National Postal Museum’s Delivering the Hope Diamond.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin hold a news conference calling for a “bold direction” for Senate Democrats on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

It has been revealed that more Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., to lead their conference in the majority.

Industry observers note that but Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., publicly calling for a different leader or a “concrete plan” that provides change.

“I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it.”.

Sanders said during a news conference Tuesday the election was about “change and the need for the Democratic Party to move in a upcoming and bold direction.”.

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders remarked, calling for an “economy that works for all, not just the people on top.”.

According to recent reports, “Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction?” he asked. “No.”.

Recent findings suggest that some incoming members and now incumbents have pointed to Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen as one possibility to challenge Schumer. Van Hollen had previously thrown cold water on the idea by saying he was instead “kicking the tires” on a presidential run in 2028 but has recently changed his tune.

A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking noted he “has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode.”.

Slotkin did not endorse anyone for leader but remarked she had a “really productive conversation” with Van Hollen yesterday.

Sources indicate that “Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete initiative that’s definitely different. I’m a ‘no’ until and unless I see that from anyone,” she remarked, urging her peers to “withhold quorum” when Senate Democrats hold their leadership elections “until you get that plan and you feel like you have a voice in that plan.”.

She urged not just a roadmap for the first 100 days, but ideas for how to “communicate differently.” As for her own future, she said, “I am not actively seeking this job. I’m seeking change.”.

Asked about his prepares Monday evening, Van Hollen stated, “It’s not about me, but I am listening to the thousands of people who have been calling for change, but especially listening to our members, with a particular ear to fresh members who have just come off the campaign trail.”.

In a recent development, “What I’ve said from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. According to recent reports, van Hollen took it a step further at an event Tuesday in Washington, D.C., criticizing the minority leader and Democrats’ campaign arm over their preferences in some primaries. “Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates,” he said, according to a livestream of the event.

In a recent development, schumer tried to tamp down the suggestion of a rivalry. “We talk frequently, and we’re united — united in lowering costs, and united in ending this damn war,” he mentioned of Van Hollen.

Others threw their support behind Schumer ahead of the Democratic leadership elections, which are expected to take place in December.

Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., praised Schumer for raising money and recruiting candidates like Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Roy Cooper of North Carolina to help land at minimum seven seats, and potentially nine if Alaska and Mississippi ultimately swing their way.

“That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership, and that is what Sen. Schumer has done. And that is why you will see, despite all grumblings, enormous gratitude,” she mentioned.

Gillibrand pointed to candidates like Scott Colom, the Democrat in Mississippi who is presently leading GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a nail-biter of a race. “That wave doesn’t get created by magic. It gets created by hard work and putting the pieces together over years,” she said.

Colom, however, has been noncommittal, telling MS NOW, “Too many of our leaders are from the same areas of the country,” pointing to the Brooklyn roots of both Schumer and current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to run for speaker on the House side.

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., stated he and Schumer have had their differences. But he implied he backs him for majority leader: “At the end of the day, these are historic numbers. It’s time for us to unify. We are going to work together as a caucus to plan together about how to move forward for what the country wants us to do, and I think we have the person who I think is going to lead us there.”.

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., said Democrats have “an opportunity to do things differently, and I think we will, regardless of who the leader is. It doesn’t really matter whose name is on the door.”.

It has been revealed that “Yes,” he remarked of his support for Schumer, noting that so far, nobody has officially stepped up to the plate. “This is a guy that worked incredibly hard over the last couple of years. I know people have other opinions about this. But we have a mandate to do things and get things done for the American people.”.

“And we can do that with Chuck Schumer.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Teton hunters must use non-lead ammunition, carry bear spray and turn in every elk head for chronic wasting disease testing. Visitors should wear bright colors.

In Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming, a small number of licensed hunters are allowed to take elk inside the park until December 6.

The annual elk reduction program runs from November 14 through December 6, according to the National Park Service.

It is authorized under the park’s 1950 enabling legislation and managed jointly by the Park Service and the Wyoming Game and Fish Department.

This year, only 40 permits are authorized, and hunters may take only cows and calves.

After reviewing available biological data, the Park Service and Wyoming Game and Fish determined that the program is necessary “to maintain the herd at its population objective and achieve desired elk distribution,” according to the Park Service.

According to recent reports, the program uses Wyoming-licensed hunters with limited-quota permits to harvest elk in designated areas. The Park Service calls it “an important management tool with requirements that distinguish it from traditional elk hunting programs.”.

Participants must carry a state license for Elk Hunt Area 75, a conservation stamp, an elk special management permit, a 2026 park elk reduction program permit and a hunter education card, regardless of age.

Sources indicate that they must use non-lead ammunition and wear fluorescent orange or pink clothing. They also have to carry bear spray that is immediately accessible, in a non-expired can of at least 7.9 ounces.

Archery equipment, handguns, non-centerfire rifles and artificial elk calls are prohibited, the Park Service says.

Only Area 75 is open for the program this year. It lies mostly east of U.S. Highway 89, according to the park.

Within Area 75, the Antelope Flats portion and the Snake River bottom between Deadman’s Bar and Ditch Creek are closed throughout the season.

Area 79 is closed to the program this season “to limit harvest pressure on northern migratory and resident elk,” the park states.

To support surveillance for chronic wasting disease, known as CWD, participants must turn in the head of every elk harvested in the park at the designated drop-off location in Moose.

Park staff collect lymph nodes and send them to the Wyoming Game and Fish Wildlife Health Lab for testing, and hunters can check their results online.

In a recent development, elk face other health threats too. Earth.com has reported on an emerging hoof disease that may change how elk bodies work.

The areas remain open to park visitors during the program, the Park Service states, and visitors are “strongly encouraged to wear bright colors.”.

Park Service and Wyoming Game and Fish staff patrol the area to check that hunters follow the rules and to share information about bear safety.

It has been revealed that hunters are not the only pressure on elk in the region. In nearby Yellowstone, research suggests cougars pose an even bigger threat to elk than wolves.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service news release 2026 Elk Reduction Program begins November 14 in Grand Teton National Park (November 6, 2026) and Grand Teton National Park’s Elk Reduction Area 75 page.

Why does sleep get worse with age? A common vitamin deficiency may offer a clue

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A study of 460 adults found that people with vitamin D deficiency slept 23 minutes less each night than those with normal levels.
  • In a recent development, sleep often becomes shorter and more fragmented as people age.
  • Among middle-aged and older adults, higher vitamin D concentrations were associated with longer sleep at night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A study of 460 adults found that people with vitamin D deficiency slept 23 minutes less each night than those with normal levels.

In a recent development, sleep often becomes shorter and more fragmented as people age. A fresh study has examined whether the level of vitamin D in the blood is related to that change.

Among middle-aged and older adults, higher vitamin D concentrations were associated with longer sleep at night. Episodes of waking during the night were also found to be shorter.

Sources indicate that the largest difference was observed in participants whose vitamin D was low enough to meet the definition of deficiency. These individuals slept about 23 minutes less per night than participants with normal levels.

The analysis was led by Diefei Chen, a PhD candidate in the Department of Epidemiology. This department forms part of the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

According to recent reports, researchers from the National Institute on Aging were also involved in the work. Because the design was observational, an association could be identified but a causal effect could not be established.

Industry observers note that most vitamin D in the human body is synthesized in the skin following exposure to sunlight. Additional amounts are supplied through diet and through supplements.

In a recent development, receptors for the vitamin are present in the brain. They are found in high numbers within a small region that regulates the body’s daily rhythm of sleep and waking.

Deficiency is also common among older adults in the United States. According to the estimates cited by the authors, roughly half of this population has low levels.

Recent findings suggest that disturbed sleep is reported by more than half of older Americans. Such sleep problems have been associated with greater risks of illness and death.

According to recent reports, in a 2015 study of 3,048 older men, low vitamin D was linked to shorter and less efficient sleep. Whether the same relationship would hold in women had not been determined.

Participants were drawn from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, an ongoing project that follows healthy adults as they age.

According to recent reports, data collected between 2012 and 2019 were used. The final sample consisted of 460 adults aged 40 years or older with a mean age of about 71.

It has been revealed that women made up slightly more than half of the sample. Approximately one participant in five was Black.

Industry observers note that inclusion was limited to people whose memory and thinking were normal. Individuals with dementia or milder forms of cognitive impairment were excluded at the outset.

Such conditions can disturb sleep in their own right, and poor nutrition linked to them may lower vitamin levels.

A fasting blood sample was obtained from each participant and analyzed for vitamin D and vitamin B12.

Each participant was also asked to wear a small motion sensor on the non-dominant wrist for seven full days.

Over the same week, bedtimes, rising times and any daytime naps were logged by the participants in a sleep diary.

Sleep averaged approximately 6 hours and 40 minutes per night, with about 48 minutes awake after sleep onset.

For the main comparison, participants were sorted by vitamin D concentration into three groups of similar size.

Age, sex, race, education, body weight, depressive symptoms and other medical conditions were taken into account in the models.

Following these adjustments, the highest group was found to sleep about 19 minutes longer per night than the lowest group.

A slightly greater proportion of time in bed was spent asleep by this group. Their waking episodes during the night were also somewhat shorter.

Although 19 minutes may seem modest for one night, the difference amounts to more than two hours weekly.

Industry observers note that the researchers then grouped participants using clinical thresholds. In this analysis, concentrations below 20 nanograms per milliliter were classified as deficient and those above 30 as normal.

Using these categories, deficient participants slept approximately 23 minutes less per night than those within the normal range.

Participants with concentrations between the two thresholds did not differ clearly from the normal group.

Vitamin D supplement use was reported by nearly half of the volunteers. Its inclusion in the analysis did not materially alter the results.

The association between vitamin D and sleep appeared stronger among Black participants than in the rest of the sample.

According to recent reports, black participants in the middle and highest vitamin D groups spent a greater proportion of their time in bed asleep. This proportion was about three percentage points higher than in the lowest group.

Among White participants and those of other races, the corresponding difference was smaller and may have arisen by chance.

It has been revealed that this finding was described by the authors as exploratory. Confirmation in other populations will be required.

“Black adults in the United States have a higher prevalence of vitamin D deficiency and sleep disturbances compared to white adults, and may benefit more from increasing vitamin D levels,” Chen mentioned.

Vitamin B12 was also assessed because of its role in the processes by which cells maintain DNA.

In the sample as a whole, no clear association was detected between B12 concentrations and any sleep measure.

A possible difference between the sexes was nevertheless noted. Women with higher B12 concentrations spent slightly less time awake during the night.

An opposite pattern was seen in men, although that estimate was too imprecise to be distinguished from chance.

Low B12 concentrations were identified in only 14 participants, so a modest effect may have gone undetected.

Industry observers note that most participants were assessed on a single occasion. Changes in sleep therefore could not be tracked as vitamin D concentrations rose or fell.

In a recent development, the direction of the association remains uncertain. Poor sleep could lead to lower vitamin D rather than the reverse.

It has been revealed that low vitamin D may also act as a general indicator of declining health. The sources of each participant’s vitamin D could not be distinguished.

The cohort was relatively healthy, and the results may not apply to less healthy populations.

In a recent development, wrist sensors are also limited in what they record. The time spent in individual sleep stages cannot be measured with such devices.

Adam Spira, a professor in the Department of Mental Health at the Bloomberg School, served as senior author.

“These findings suggest that we should investigate more thoroughly whether boosting vitamin D levels can improve sleep health,” Spira stated.

According to recent reports, earlier trials have reported that vitamin D supplements improved self-rated sleep. Those assessments were based on questionnaires rather than on sensor recordings.

The next question is whether raising vitamin D would lengthen sleep as recorded by a sensor. Future studies in older adults could test this directly.

The full study was published in The Journals of Gerontology: Series A.

It has been revealed that sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take. Proteins typically studied in the brain were turning up in prostate cancer cells from high-risk patients. These proteins, called neuronal adhesion molecules, play a key role in the circuitry associated with memory.

The finding, made during her Ph.D. days at the University of Illinois Chicago, raised so many questions to which Eksi is still seeking answers. Now at the Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Eksi has made it her lab’s goal to find out how nervous systems communicate with cancer. What were once two separate fields might be connected more closely than previously thought.

Recent findings suggest that “What we’re learning is that tumors are actively communicating with the nervous system,” Eksi notes. “In a way, it makes sense to me that a growing tumor in our bodies, in an organ, would be immediately sensed and detected by the nervous system.”.

Eksi now aims to test an AI image-based recognition algorithm to identify nerve fibers in human patients. This is exciting, she says, because these nerves aren’t normally visible in patient tumors. But through biopsies, she hopes to map out and observe how the nervous system — which impacts sleep, cognition and pain — changes as cancer progresses. The implications are significant, she says. Could experts use the nervous system to detect cancer early? Can they improve patients’ quality of life?

According to recent reports, “This field of cancer neuroscience can change all different stages of cancer diagnosis and treatments,” Eksi notes. “It’s growing so rapidly, the field itself.”.

Quitting statins after age 70 initially appeared to be safe, yet heart attacks, strokes, and deaths increased after four years off those meds

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A trial of adults aged 70 and older without cardiovascular disease found that stopping preventive statins may carry greater long-term risks.
  • When adults aged 70 and older stopped taking statins for preventing a first heart attack or stroke, they did not see a significant jump in heart attacks, strokes, or deaths two years later.
  • A research team followed participants for a median of 103 weeks, and up to four years for some.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A trial of adults aged 70 and older without cardiovascular disease found that stopping preventive statins may carry greater long-term risks.

When adults aged 70 and older stopped taking statins for preventing a first heart attack or stroke, they did not see a significant jump in heart attacks, strokes, or deaths two years later.

A research team followed participants for a median of 103 weeks, and up to four years for some.

It has been revealed that during that time, 12.7 percent of the group that stopped taking statins suffered a heart attack, a stroke, or death. That compares with 9.2 percent of the group that continued taking them.

In a recent development, the results were presented on Nov. 7, 2026, at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions in Chicago and published the same day.

Named STREAM, the trial enrolled 1,880 adults aged 70 or older with no known cardiovascular disease. The name stands for statin discontinuation as prevention among the elderly and multimorbid.

Every participant was taking a statin to lower cholesterol as primary prevention. That term means the drug is meant to head off a first such event, not a second one.

Each also had at least two chronic conditions, such as a past cancer or lung disease. The average age was 77, and 47 percent of the group were women.

Of those enrolled, 938 were randomly assigned to stop the drug and 942 to carry on.

Sources indicate that STREAM ran from November 2021 to April 2026 at 24 clinical centers in Switzerland, France and the Netherlands. Hospitals in Bern, Lausanne, Geneva, Zurich and Basel were among the Swiss sites.

The main outcome combined three events: a nonfatal heart attack, a nonfatal ischemic stroke, or death from any cause.

It has been revealed that during the first two years, 100 people in the group that stopped and 77 in the group that continued had one of them. That works out to 10.7 percent against 8.2 percent.

According to recent reports, STREAM was built as a noninferiority trial, a design that asks whether stopping is not meaningfully worse than continuing. The two-year difference stayed within the limit set in advance.

Outcomes were judged by reviewers who did not know which group a patient belonged to, according to the University of Bern, which led the project.

Patients and their doctors knew the assignment, because STREAM was run open-label.

According to recent reports, its rationale was that the value of these drugs is uncertain after age 70 in people with no heart disease. Side effects and risky combinations of drugs are also common in that age group.

Recent findings suggest that across the full follow-up, 119 events occurred among those who had stopped, against 87 among those who had continued. The counts come from the AHA’s late-breaking science report.

The design centered on the two-year comparison.

According to recent reports, nicolas Rodondi led the work. He is professor of primary care and internal medicine and director of the Institute of Primary Health Care at the University of Bern.

He estimated that over two years, one additional major cardiovascular event or death would occur for every 40 people who stopped their statin.

The association’s report notes that the estimate requires further investigation.

It has been revealed that A second set of measures looked at how people felt. Pain, quality of life, fall risk and muscle weakness indicated no difference between the two groups.

According to recent reports, sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength that comes with age, was also no more common in one group than the other. Reports of muscle pain were no different either.

Roughly 14 percent of participants crossed over along the way. Some who had stopped restarted, and some who had continued quit.

Extra analyses that took those switches into account did not change the result.

“Our findings provide information for shared decision-making about cautious statin discontinuation when statins are used for primary prevention only,” Rodondi stated.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) advises a statin for some adults aged 40 to 75. They must have at least one risk factor and a 10-year cardiovascular risk of 10 percent or more.

When that risk falls between 7.5 percent and 10 percent, it tells clinicians to offer the drug selectively, because the likely benefit is smaller.

Sources indicate that for adults 76 and older, the task force concluded that the evidence is insufficient to weigh the benefits and harms of starting one. The recommendation dates from August 2022 and replaced a 2016 version.

Sources indicate that its advice turns on a patient’s overall risk, not on LDL cholesterol alone, and it addresses starting a statin. STREAM tested the opposite question: what happens when older adults already on a statin stop.

“Although deprescribing inappropriate drugs in older adults appears to be safe, the results of our trial suggest that additional randomized trials of discontinuation are needed for specific drugs,” Rodondi noted.

The study was published in the journal The Fresh England Journal of Medicine.

Astronauts could turn everyday trash and moon dust into something surprisingly useful

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have combined paper fibers and simulated lunar dust to develop lightweight insulation that could be manufactured on the moon.
  • Trash on the International Space Station is bagged by astronauts and loaded onto a cargo ship.
  • According to recent reports, the ship then either returns it to Earth or burns up in the atmosphere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have combined paper fibers and simulated lunar dust to develop lightweight insulation that could be manufactured on the moon.

Trash on the International Space Station is bagged by astronauts and loaded onto a cargo ship.

According to recent reports, the ship then either returns it to Earth or burns up in the atmosphere. On the moon, part of that waste might be put to use as insulation.

Paper fibers have now been ground together with imitation moon dust by a team of chemists.

The mixture was dried into an aerogel, an ultralight solid made mostly of empty space. Very little heat passes through such a material.

Sources indicate that according to the results, some insulation for a lunar base could be made on site. Two ingredients would be needed, and both should be plentiful there: waste paper and the ground outside.

Industry observers note that the recipe was developed by Alexander Wei, a chemistry professor at Purdue University, and graduate researcher Jacob Staker. Their colleagues included researchers at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland.

Wei said a lunar settlement will generate waste rich in cellulose, the plant fiber found in paper and cardboard packaging.

“And I can guarantee that astronauts on the moon will never run out of moon dust,” Wei added.

For now, the aerogels exist only as samples made on Earth. A manufactured stand-in was used for lunar soil, and the paper was clean laboratory filter paper.

The final drying step relied on a method the team considers less practical on the moon than freeze-drying.

In a recent development, between 60% and 70% of wastepaper by weight is cellulose. When cellulose is torn into much finer threads, it can strengthen a material in ways the original fibers cannot.

A stand-in for lunar soil, or regolith, has already been mixed with recycled plastic by other engineers. Wei’s team paired the dust with paper instead and used it as a grinding aid.

According to recent reports, filter paper was first shredded in a food blender. The team then loaded it into a mill together with water, ceramic cylinders, and a powder called Lunar Highlands Simulant.

This powder is made from Earth rock to match soil from the moon’s highlands.

For two hours, the jars were spun at an acceleration about 60 times that of Earth’s gravity.

The team expects a mill of this kind to work in the moon’s weak gravity.

The paper fibers were thinned by the ceramic cylinders alone. Once dust was added, they became much thinner still.

The most common fiber width fell to about 4 millionths of an inch (0.1 micrometers).

According to recent reports, fibers milled with dust were eight times thinner than those milled without it. They were also at least 30 times thinner than the original paper fibers.

The milled mixture was frozen in small molds, and its water was replaced with alcohol.

The team then removed the alcohol with pressurized carbon dioxide, which is a standard way of drying aerogels.

In a recent development, “Imagine an aerogel as a high-tech thermos for a lunar base,” Staker remarked. “Most of it consists of empty space that insulates the interior, helping it maintain the temperature of what’s inside.”.

Empty space accounted for 79.3% to 98.6% of the volume in these samples.

According to recent reports, in total, 18 batches were made, and the recipe was varied between them. Cellulose made up 1% to 9% of the wet mixture by weight. Dust made up 25% to 75% of the finished aerogel.

Industry observers note that insulation is rated by its thermal conductivity, which describes how easily heat passes through a material. A lower value is better.

The batches scored between 30 and 45 milliwatts per meter-kelvin when measured in air.

An earlier attempt had produced a freeze-dried aerogel of imitation regolith and natural polymers. Its lowest reported figure was 70 in the same units.

The best upcoming batches therefore had less than half the thermal conductivity of the earlier material.

The best insulation came from the batches with the least cellulose. Among the 18, the lightest batch was made from a mixture with 1% cellulose. Its conductivity of 30.9 was the lowest in that group.

When exposed to the moon’s near-vacuum environment, the pores would contain virtually no gas.

Industry observers note that the team expects the aerogels to insulate better under those conditions. Several times less heat is conducted by other aerospace aerogels in a near-vacuum than in air.

Temperatures on the lunar surface can reach 266°F (130°C). That heat is a problem for many of the organic materials used in aerogels.

A sample heated in nitrogen did not start to break down until about 653°F (345°C).

In a recent development, insulation and stiffness responded to the recipe in opposite ways. Heat was generally blocked best by the low-cellulose batches.

However, those batches were also soft, and they shrank the most during drying.

Recent findings suggest that A batch made with 1% cellulose came out 52% narrower than its mold. Only 3.2% shrinkage was seen in a batch made with 9% cellulose.

Recent findings suggest that the stiffest batch was also made with 9% cellulose. Under compression, it was nearly 300 times stiffer than the softest batch.

“Rather than trying to make the world’s best aerogel, we’re looking for the sweet spot where we can get the properties we need with the limited resources we have available,” Wei said.

Industry observers note that to look for that balance, the team fitted a statistical model to the 18 batches. Three recipes suggested by the model were then made and tested.

It has been revealed that dust would be far more plentiful on the moon than waste paper. For that reason, one recipe was required to be at least 60% dust by weight.

In a recent development, A figure of 61.2% was suggested by the model. The resulting aerogel had a conductivity of 30.5, which was the lowest in the study.

The same aerogel shrank by about half. It also did not meet the standards for the strength test.

A second recipe was balanced across six measured properties. It insulated nearly as well, at 30.8, and shrank by 18.5%. This aerogel was stiff enough to be tested, but only 25% of it was dust.

It has been revealed that the aerogels have not yet been made the way a lunar crew would make them. The team wrote that freeze-drying would be far more practical on the moon than the carbon dioxide method.

According to Wei, the lunar surface offers a natural vacuum and subfreezing temperatures at night. Wei noted the water removed from the aerogel could also be recovered and reused.

Industry observers note that however, this kind of material can be damaged by freezing. Growing ice crystals pack the fibers and dust together.

According to recent reports, that packing is known to lower the quality of cellulose aerogels. To slow the growth of the crystals, the team proposed adding simple alcohols or sugars.

According to recent reports, only one kind of imitation dust was used, and the paper was not real trash. Every heat-flow measurement was taken at 73°F (23°C) in air.

For the weakest recipes, additives known to strengthen cellulose aerogels should be tested, the team suggested.

Recent findings suggest that freeze-drying is now being studied by the team for its next batches. Those tests should show whether a freeze-dried aerogel can insulate as well as the samples made so far.

The full study was published in the journal ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering.

Flying squirrels have an unusual habit that may shape entire forests

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Flying squirrels in China may influence where young trees grow by storing nuts in branches instead of underground.
  • Squirrels help oak forests grow by burying acorns and forgetting about them.
  • Instead of burying nuts, they tuck them between small branches.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Flying squirrels in China may influence where young trees grow by storing nuts in branches instead of underground.

Squirrels help oak forests grow by burying acorns and forgetting about them. But two species of flying squirrel in southern China have a different way of storing food.

Instead of burying nuts, they tuck them between small branches. A fresh study suggests that this habit may affect where young trees grow.

Sources indicate that researchers found fewer seedlings a short distance from parent trees. But their numbers increased again about 66 feet (20 meters) away, where squirrels often store their nuts.

Industry observers note that scientists have usually linked this pattern to tree diseases. The latest study suggests that squirrels may also play a role.

The work was carried out by Xuelian Tan, Han Xu and their colleagues at the Research Institute of Tropical Forestry. This institute is part of the Chinese Academy of Forestry in Guangzhou.

Industry observers note that the study was a field survey of two tree species in a single forest. It therefore highlights a match between stored nuts and seedlings rather than proof that the squirrels planted them.

The research took place in Jianfengling, a forest within the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park on Hainan Island.

In a recent development, the forest averages about 67°F (19.7°C), and about 97 inches (2,461 millimeters) of rain falls there each year. In total, 992 species of free-standing trees and shrubs have been recorded in the forest.

Two of these trees are Cyclobalanopsis edithiae and Cyclobalanopsis patelliformis, which are close relatives of oaks. Their nuts are smooth and are not covered by the small cup at their base.

Sources indicate that many animals feed on these nuts. Their slick surfaces make them difficult to hold in place on a branch, however.

The flying squirrels solve this problem by gnawing grooves into the nuts, allowing them to wedge their food between branches.

The grooves differ between the two kinds of nut. Oval C. edithiae nuts usually receive one zigzag groove around the middle. Flatter C. patelliformis nuts, on the other hand, may carry up to 20 grooves on the underside.

Most stored nuts sat 33 to 82 feet (10 to 25 meters) from the nearest possible parent tree. Photographs in the upcoming study show squirrels returning to collect their nuts.

Another image highlights a gnawed nut that had fallen to the forest floor and begun to sprout.

Recent findings suggest that the importance of this behavior is linked to an older idea about how tropical forests work. During the early 1970s, the ecologists Daniel Janzen and Joseph Connell observed a pattern among tree seedlings.

In a recent development, young trees, they noticed, were seldom found close to adults of their own species. The pair put this down to disease and pests.

Fungi and plant-eating insects that target one tree species spread from an adult tree to the seedlings around it.

Sources indicate that seedlings close to the parent are therefore more likely to die. Most seeds, however, land near the parent tree in the first place.

When both effects are combined, most surviving seedlings would be expected at a middle distance from the parent.

Recent findings suggest that ecologists refer to this process as conspecific negative density dependence. In simpler terms, plants tend to do poorly when they are surrounded by their own species.

Industry observers note that this effect helps prevent any single species from dominating a forest. It is one reason why a rainforest can support so many different kinds of trees.

An earlier study in one of the Jianfengling plots detected the effect in 89% of tree species.

Industry observers note that where a seedling ends up hinges on two separate events. A seed has to land somewhere, and the young plant has to survive in that spot.

Seed-carrying animals can shift the first of these. Whether they could mimic the disease pattern on their own had gone largely untested.

Twenty parent trees anchored the survey. On ten of them, squirrels had lodged nuts in at least one direction.

The other ten were bare on all four sides. Each of the first ten trees got two survey lines.

One pointed toward the stashed nuts, and the second ran off where no nuts hung. A single line from each bare tree, comparable in trunk size, formed a second point of comparison.

Markers went down every 16 feet (5 meters), stopping at roughly 100 feet (30 meters). Beside each marker lay three plots about a yard (1 meter) square. Every seedling inside those plots was tallied.

Seedlings along the test lines were most plentiful beside the parent tree. Their numbers, however, fell away at 16 and 33 feet (5 and 10 meters).

According to recent reports, at 49 and 66 feet (15 and 20 meters), on the other hand, the counts climbed once more. Farther out they declined again, and the comparison lines highlighted no second rise at all.

Recent findings suggest that the 66-foot mark stood out in particular. There, the test lines held more seedlings than both comparison groups. The difference was statistically significant.

In a recent development, this is, notably, the very band of distances in which the squirrels hang their nuts. Beside the trunk itself, the test lines also held more seedlings, though only relative to the second group.

The authors offered a simple explanation, namely that trees ignored by squirrels may produce fewer nuts. Fewer nuts would mean fewer seedlings and, in turn, fewer squirrel visits.

Comparisons on two sides of the same tree therefore mattered, since seedling numbers vary widely from tree to tree.

Disease, for its part, ought to leave more damage on saplings close to the parent. Fine roots from 33 young trees were therefore examined, 15 of one species and 18 of the other.

The trees grew at different distances from adults. Each sapling’s root samples were inspected at 100 points under a microscope for lesions, which can indicate infection.

The level of damage, however, demonstrated no clear trend with distance.

Recent findings suggest that fungi are not cleared by this result. Root lesions, the authors wrote, may not reflect the full pressure that pathogens place on seedlings.

They also wrote that “our results do not imply that pathogens are unimportant.”.

Squirrels that move nuts are, in their account, one more possible influence on where seedlings take root.

Industry observers note that tan and Xu’s team has not confirmed whether squirrels directly help new trees grow. Other animals and local growing conditions may also play a role.

Changing how squirrels store nuts could provide stronger evidence, but such experiments are difficult in the wild.

It has been revealed that the researchers suggest tracking seedlings over several years to see whether the nuts grow into healthy trees. Future studies could also examine other animals and forests.

The full study was published in the journal Forest Ecosystems.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In a recent development, yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.

“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” notes Yin, of Cornell University.

Industry observers note that he applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.

“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin states, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”.

More recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the glitch in a measurable way, Yin says.

“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin indicates.
